Source: [Apple Podcasts artwork requirements](https://podcasters.apple.com/support/artwork-requirements).

#### Cover art, episode art, and video thumbnails compared

Podcast cover art is the required image for the whole show. Episode art is an optional image that replaces the cover for one episode in supported apps. Video episodes can also use a widescreen thumbnail.

| Image | Required? | Where it appears | Open Tab example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Podcast cover art: one square image for the show | Yes | Show pages, search results, charts, listeners’ libraries, and episodes without their own art | The orange-red OPEN TAB square |
| Episode art: one square image for an episode | No | That episode’s listing and player in supported apps, such as Apple Podcasts | None; all Open Tab episodes use the show cover |
| Video thumbnail: a 16:9 image for a video episode | No | Substack and YouTube before playback | A photo of each conversation with OPEN TAB lettering |

Use episode art to highlight a guest or mark a special series. Without it, the episode displays the show cover. On Substack, you add episode art when publishing an episode.

Open Tab’s Esther Perel video thumbnail uses orange-red OPEN TAB lettering over a photo of a conversation at a bar, with receipt-style lines below. Reusing the show’s lettering and color makes the thumbnail recognizable.

For how artwork reaches podcast apps, see [podcast RSS feeds](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### Podcast cover art examples by show type

Choose a style based on what listeners come for: a person, a subject, or a story. Look at leading shows in your category. Genre-appropriate artwork helps listeners understand what to expect before reading anything.

| Show type | Visual approach | What it tells listeners |
|---|---|---|
| Host-led or interview show | Clear photo of the host’s face, with the name in large type | “You are listening to this person” |
| Co-hosted conversation | Both hosts cropped close, or two illustrated portraits | “Two voices, a conversation” |
| Topic or expert show | Bold typography on a solid color, or one strong subject-related symbol | “This is about [subject]” |
| Fan or community show | An image or color scheme fans recognize | “Made by fans, for fans” |
| Fiction or storytelling | An illustration or photograph that establishes the mood | “A story, in this genre” |
| Narrated newsletter | The publication’s existing logo, colors, and type | “The audio version of something you already read” |

### Free podcast cover art templates

[Canva](https://www.canva.com/podcast-covers/templates/) and [Adobe Express](https://www.adobe.com/express/templates/cover/podcast) offer free plans with square podcast-cover templates you can edit with your own title, colors, and images.

For a no-budget launch, see [how to start a podcast for free](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/for-free).

### How to make podcast cover art step by step

1. **Create a 3000 × 3000 pixel square canvas.** Use a template or a blank square in any design tool.
2. **Choose one main image or symbol.** One clear image works better at small sizes than several. Open Tab uses its large title as the image, without a photo.
3. **Choose a high-contrast background.** Use a light background behind a dark title, or the reverse. Open Tab uses pale pink letters on solid orange-red.
4. **Set the title in large, simple type.** It should fill much of the square. Avoid thin or script fonts, which are difficult to read at small sizes. OPEN and TAB occupy most of Open Tab’s cover.
5. **Leave empty space around the edges.** Keep the title and main image away from the corners and bottom edge. Open Tab leaves a solid-color border around its text.
6. **Check the design at thumbnail size.** Zoom out until it is about the size of an app icon. If the title is unreadable, enlarge or shorten it.
7. **Export as a JPEG or PNG in RGB color.**
8. **Make a 16:9 version for video, if needed.** Rearrange the same elements on a 1920 × 1080 pixel canvas, as Open Tab does for its episode thumbnails.

### Check readability, image rights, and export quality

#### Readability

- Shrink the cover to phone-app-icon size and confirm the title is readable.
- Check it against both light and dark backgrounds, including how it looks in dark mode.
- Keep important elements out of corners and away from the bottom edge.

Open Tab’s solid orange-red square stands out against both light and dark screens.

#### Image and font rights

- Use photos you took, illustrations you made, or images licensed for commercial use.
- Check that each stock-image and font license covers use on a podcast cover. Free-image sites and Creative Commons licenses have differing terms; read the terms for each image.
- Leave out other brands’ logos, TV or film stills, album art, and photos of people who have not agreed to appear.
- For AI-generated images, check that the tool’s terms permit commercial use.

For a specific licensing question, read the license itself or ask a lawyer.

#### Export quality

- Export a square between 1400 × 1400 and 3000 × 3000 pixels.
- Save as JPEG or PNG in RGB color at 72 dpi.
- Open the exported file at full size and check for blurring, pixelation, and text cut off at the edges.

### Upload your podcast cover art and check the result

On Substack, upload your show cover when setting up the podcast. Substack includes it in the RSS feed so it appears on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other podcast apps.

1. Open your **Dashboard** and select **Podcast**.
2. Upload the cover art in your podcast details.
3. Select **Create podcast**.

Until you upload custom artwork, Substack uses a default microphone drawing—a white microphone on a green tile. Replace it before submitting the show to Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

**Episode art on Substack:** On an episode’s Publish page, open **Episode metadata** and upload an image under **Episode art**. Supported podcast apps use it for that episode. A guest photo or episode-specific design should use the same size and format as the show cover.

#### Check the published result

- Open the show in the Substack app and on your publication’s podcast page.
- On a phone, check the cover in Apple Podcasts and Spotify search results and your library.
- Allow time for changes to appear. Substack updates the RSS feed immediately, but Apple Podcasts and Spotify can take up to **24 hours** to display a new cover.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What size should podcast cover art be?

A square between 1400 × 1400 and 3000 × 3000 pixels. Export at 3000 × 3000 pixels in JPEG or PNG format and RGB color.

#### What file format should podcast cover art be?

JPEG or PNG, in RGB color at 72 dpi. CMYK files, intended for print, can display incorrectly in podcast apps.

#### Is podcast cover art the same on Spotify and Apple Podcasts?

Yes. Both use the square cover from the RSS feed, so one 3000 × 3000 pixel file works on both.

#### Do I need different cover art for each episode?

No. Episode art is optional. Without it, apps show the show cover for every episode. Separate episode art can highlight a guest or special series.

#### Should I put the word “podcast” on my cover art?

No. Podcast apps already communicate the format, and the space is better used for a larger title.

#### Can I make podcast cover art for free?

Yes. Free design tools with podcast templates, combined with your own photos or illustrations, are enough to make cover art meeting every platform’s requirements.

### Starting a podcast on Substack

The page states that you can start a podcast for free on Substack, with no hosting fees or platform fees. Upload the artwork once for distribution to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and subscribers.

## How to edit a podcast with free software

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/editing

Edit your first episode in a free audio editor, from cutting mistakes to exporting a file you can publish.

Last updated: October 22, 2026 · By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack

### What does podcast editing involve?

Podcast editing turns a raw recording into an episode that is easy to listen to. You can edit a podcast for free in six steps:

1. Choose free podcast editing software and prepare your project.
2. Cut mistakes while keeping the conversation natural.
3. Reduce noise without damaging speech.
4. Balance voices and add transitions.
5. Export your episode and listen to the final file.
6. Upload your episode to Substack.

This guide is part of the [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### Choose free podcast editing software and prepare your project

Two free editors cover everything a beginner needs:

| Editor | Cost | Works on | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Audacity](https://www.audacityteam.org/) | Free and open source | Windows, Mac, and Linux | Full editing, with noise reduction and volume tools |
| [GarageBand](https://www.apple.com/mac/garageband/) | Free | Mac, iPhone, and iPad | Simple cuts and music on Apple devices |

Descript and Riverside also have free plans with limits. Descript's free plan includes **60 minutes of media a month**, and Riverside's free plan records a separate track for each speaker for your **first 2 hours of recordings**.

The steps below use Audacity because it is free on Windows, Mac, and Linux. To prepare your project:

1. Download Audacity from the [Audacity website](https://www.audacityteam.org/download/) and install it.
2. Make a copy of your recording file and edit the copy, so the original stays unchanged.
3. Open Audacity and drag the file onto the window, or select **File > Import**.
4. Listen to the whole recording once on headphones, and write down the time of anything you want to cut or fix.

### Cut mistakes while keeping the conversation natural

Cut false starts, long silences, and anything that distracts the listener, but leave natural pauses and small slips. Listeners expect a conversation, not a perfect reading.

To cut a section in Audacity:

1. Click in the waveform where the section starts, and drag to where it ends.
2. Press **Delete**. The first time you delete, Audacity asks what to do with the gap. Choose **Close gap**, so the audio after the cut moves back to fill it.
3. Play a few seconds before and after the cut, and check that it sounds smooth.

To shorten long pauses all at once, select the whole recording and choose **Effect > Special > Truncate silence**. Audacity finds every silence longer than the length you set and shortens it.

In GarageBand on a Mac, move the playhead to where a cut starts and choose **Edit > Split Regions at Playhead**. Split again where the cut ends, then select the part in between and press **Delete**. On an iPhone or iPad, tap the region, then tap **Split**.

### Reduce noise without damaging speech

Noise reduction lowers steady background sounds, such as the hum of a fan or a computer. It works best on gentle, constant noise, and **cannot remove a dog barking or a door closing**.

1. Select a few seconds of the recording where no one is speaking and you hear only the background noise.
2. Choose **Effect > Noise removal and repair > Noise reduction**, and select **Get noise profile**.
3. Select the whole recording, open **Noise reduction** again, and apply it.
4. Listen to the result. If voices sound thin, hollow, or robotic, undo the change and try a lower setting. Some background noise left in sounds better than damaged voices.

The best fix for noise is a quieter room. See [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) for room setup guidance.

### Balance voices and add transitions

Listeners should not have to change their volume during an episode. Two Audacity effects even out the sound:

- **Loudness Normalization** (**Effect > Volume and compression > Loudness Normalization**) sets how loud the whole selection sounds to listeners. Apple Podcasts recommends an overall loudness of about **−16 LKFS**, a measure of how loud audio sounds to people. Audacity measures loudness in LUFS, which is the same unit, so set the target to **−16 LUFS**.
- **Compressor** (**Effect > Volume and compression > Compressor**) makes the loudest moments quieter, so the level of each voice stays steadier.

If one person is much quieter than another, select only that person's parts and apply Loudness Normalization to them first.

To add music, choose **Tracks > New stereo track**, then import the music file into the new track and drag it into place. To make music start and end gently, select the start of the music and choose **Effect > Fading > Fade In**, then select the end and choose **Fade Out**.

Use only music you have the right to use. For free music sources and their license terms, see [how much it costs to start a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost).

In GarageBand, drag each track's **Volume** slider to balance the voices.

### Export your episode and listen to the final file

In Audacity, choose **File > Export audio**. Name the file, choose **MP3** as the format, and choose a bit rate. The Audacity manual describes **128 kbps** as a safe default for speech.

In GarageBand on a Mac, choose **Share > Export Song to Disk**, and choose MP3, AAC, AIFF, or WAVE. On an iPhone or iPad, touch and hold the song in the My Songs browser, then tap **Share**.

Before you publish, listen to the whole exported file once. Check the beginning and the end, and listen to every place you made a cut.

#### Upload your episode to Substack

When your file is ready, you can publish it on Substack for free.

1. Select **Create**, then **Podcast**, to open a new draft episode.
2. On the draft, select **Select file** and choose your exported file. Substack accepts **MP3, WAV, and AAC** files.
3. Add your show notes. On Substack, show notes become the episode's description in Apple Podcasts and Spotify.
4. Select **Continue**, choose who gets the episode, choose whether to send it by email and in the Substack app, and publish.

#### Why publish your podcast on Substack?

Substack hosts and distributes your podcast for free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees, no matter how many subscribers you have. Every episode you upload goes to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, the Substack app, and your subscribers' inboxes, with a transcript added automatically.

If you record in the Substack Recording Studio, Substack also makes short clips you can share and a thumbnail you can change, with no extra editing.

Substack stays free until you turn on paid subscriptions. When you do, you keep **90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees**, and your paid subscribers can listen to every episode in the podcast app they already use. Creators publishing podcasts on Substack collectively earn [over $200 million a year](https://podnews.net/update/substack-podcast-tab).

To get your show onto Apple Podcasts and Spotify for the first time, see [how to submit your podcast RSS feed](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### Check your episode's transcript on Substack

Substack creates a transcript of every podcast episode automatically and shows it on the episode's post, so people who prefer to read can follow along. Before you publish, open the **Transcript** panel to check it:

- Select **Edit** to correct names and words the transcript got wrong.
- Select **Speakers** to name each person who speaks. You can type a name or choose a Substack profile.
- Upload your own transcript as a **.txt, .srt, or .vtt** file, if you already have one.
- Turn off **Show on post** if you do not want the transcript on the post.

### How much editing does your podcast need?

Most conversation shows need only a light edit: cut the mistakes, shorten long pauses, and even out the volume, so nothing distracts the listener. Shows with music, several segments, or sound effects take more time.

To decide how much to edit, listen to a few episodes of shows like yours and note what they leave in. Small slips and laughter can stay because they make the episode sound like a real conversation.

A clear outline before you record also leaves less to cut afterward. See [podcast script templates](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-script).

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can I edit a podcast for free?

Yes. Audacity is free and open source and works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, and GarageBand is free on Mac, iPhone, and iPad. Both can cut audio, change the volume, and export an MP3 file. Publishing the finished episode on Substack is free too.

#### What file format should I export my podcast in?

Export an **MP3** file. The Audacity manual describes **128 kbps** as a safe default for speech, and Substack accepts MP3, WAV, and AAC files when you upload an episode.

#### Do I need to remove every “um” and “uh”?

No. A few “ums” and “uhs” sound natural, and removing every one can make speech sound choppy. Cut the ones that interrupt a sentence or come one after another, and use Audacity's **Truncate silence** effect to shorten long pauses.

#### What is the best free podcast editing software?

For most beginners, **Audacity**: it is free and open source, works on Windows, Mac, and Linux, and includes noise reduction and loudness tools. On a Mac, iPhone, or iPad, **GarageBand** is free and simpler to learn. Descript and Riverside also have free plans, with limits.

#### Can I edit a podcast on my iPhone?

Yes. GarageBand is free on iPhone and iPad. Tap a region, then tap **Split** to cut it, and drag the **Track Volume** slider to balance voices. To export, touch and hold the song in the My Songs browser, then tap **Share**.

## Podcast equipment for beginners: what you need

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/equipment

### What equipment do you need to start a podcast?

Start with the equipment you already have, then add a microphone and headphones when you are ready to improve your sound.

*Last updated: October 22, 2026. By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack.*

To start a podcast, you need a microphone, headphones, and recording software. A phone and a pair of earbuds cover all three: the phone’s built-in microphone, the earbuds, and the Substack app, where you can use the [Substack Recording Studio](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) for free. For a more professional sound, add a USB microphone.

#### Podcast equipment list for beginners

| Equipment | What it does | Price range |
|---|---|---|
| Phone or computer | Runs your recording software | Equipment you already own |
| Recording software | Records you and your guests | $0 with the Substack Recording Studio |
| USB microphone | Plugs straight into a computer, and into many phones | About $100–$300 |
| Closed-back headphones | Let you hear yourself and your guests without sound leaking into the microphone | About $60–$200 |
| Microphone stand or boom arm | Holds the microphone at the same distance from your mouth | About $15–$40 for a desk stand, or $45–$140 for a boom arm |
| Pop filter or foam windscreen | Softens bursts of air on sounds like “p” and “b” | About $10–$85 |

Prices on this page are based on US list prices as of October 2026 for microphones and accessories widely used by podcasters.

This guide is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### What equipment do you need for a solo podcast?

A solo podcast can start at $0 and grow one piece at a time. Three setups cover most beginners:

- **A phone, for $0.** Record in the Substack app with your phone’s built-in microphone or wired earbuds with a microphone. Use a small, quiet room and hold the phone at a consistent distance from your mouth.
- **A phone with a clip-on microphone, for about $60–$280.** A clip-on, or lavalier, microphone attaches to your clothes, keeping its distance from your mouth consistent. It also keeps the microphone out of the picture when recording video.
- **A computer with a USB microphone, for about $160–$500.** A USB microphone is the upgrade that makes the most difference to sound quality. Closed-back headphones let you hear exactly what you record. Use the Substack Recording Studio on the web.

#### How to start recording a podcast on Substack for free

All three setups work with the free Recording Studio built into Substack. It also works in the Substack app for iPhone and Android.

To start on a computer:

1. Sign in to Substack, select **Create**, then **Recording studio**. The studio opens in your web browser.
2. Allow Substack to use your microphone and camera when your browser asks.
3. Check your microphone with the **Mic** control, then select **Start recording**.

For room setup and recording guidance, see [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording).

### USB or XLR: which microphone setup should you choose?

For most beginners, a USB microphone is simpler. An XLR microphone makes sense when two people record in the same room or when you plan to add more equipment later.

| What to compare | USB microphone | XLR microphone |
|---|---|---|
| How it connects | One cable to a computer, or to many phones | Connects to an audio interface or mixer, which connects to a computer |
| Extra equipment | None | An audio interface, about $90–$225 |
| Price range | About $100–$300 | About $100–$450, plus the interface |
| Good for | Solo shows and shows with remote guests | Two people in one room, or a setup you plan to expand |

Some microphones have both USB and XLR connections, letting you start with USB and add an audio interface later.

### What do you need for a two-person podcast?

The equipment depends on whether you record in different places or in the same room:

- **In different places:** Each person uses their own phone or computer, so no shared equipment is necessary. In the Substack Recording Studio, you can invite up to two guests by their Substack handle through the **Invite guests** panel. Each guest joins from a computer with a web browser or a phone with the Substack app, using their own microphone. Ask everyone to wear headphones.
- **In the same room:** Each person needs their own microphone and headphones. Two XLR microphones and an audio interface with two inputs keep each voice clear. Interfaces with one or two inputs cost about $90–$225.

### Podcast accessories to add later: headphones, stands, pop filters, and room treatment

You do not need these accessories to start. Add them when you want a more polished, professional sound:

- **Closed-back headphones: about $60–$200.** They keep sound in your ears so it does not leak into your microphone. Wear them every time you record.
- **Desk stand: about $15–$40; boom arm: about $45–$140.** Either holds the microphone at a consistent distance from your mouth to keep volume even. A boom arm also keeps the microphone off your desk.
- **Pop filter or foam windscreen: about $10–$85.** Both soften bursts of air on sounds like “p” and “b.” Some microphones include a foam windscreen.
- **Room treatment.** Start with a small room containing soft furniture, rugs, and curtains. If you still hear echo, acoustic foam panels cost about $60–$320 a pack, depending on panel size and quantity.

### What should you spend, and what should you upgrade first?

Start at $0, record a few episodes, and buy equipment only when you hear a problem it would fix. Upgrade in this order:

1. A USB microphone, ideally a dynamic one.
2. Closed-back headphones.
3. A stand or boom arm, and a pop filter or foam windscreen.
4. Room treatment, if you still hear echo.
5. An XLR microphone and audio interface, if a co-host joins you in the same room.

For full budgets, from a $0 setup to an upgraded one, see [how much it costs to start a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost).

### Is Substack free for podcasts?

Yes. The page states that starting and hosting a podcast on Substack is free, with no hosting fees or platform fees, regardless of subscriber count. Every published episode goes to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, the Substack app, and subscribers’ inboxes.

To earn money, creators can turn on paid subscriptions and receive payments directly from listeners. Creators keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees. The page reports that creators publishing podcasts on Substack collectively earn [over $200 million a year](https://podnews.net/update/substack-podcast-tab).

### Will a microphone work with my computer or phone?

- Check the microphone’s connector and your computer’s ports, such as USB-C or USB-A, and buy the appropriate cable or adapter.
- For a USB microphone connected to a phone, check the phone’s port. Phones with USB-C can usually connect with a USB-C cable. iPhones with Lightning ports need a certified cable or adapter.
- An XLR microphone needs an XLR cable and an audio interface. Ensure the interface has enough inputs for everyone recording in the same room.
- Check what is included. Some microphones come with a desk stand, cable, and foam windscreen.
- After connecting a new microphone, open the Substack Recording Studio, allow browser microphone access, and test it with the **Mic** control before recording.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can I start a podcast with just a phone?

Yes. A phone’s built-in microphone is enough to start, and the Substack app offers free recording through the Recording Studio. Record in a small, quiet room and hold the phone at a consistent distance from your mouth. A clip-on phone microphone costs about $60–$280 when you want better sound.

#### Do I need a mixer for a podcast?

No. A USB microphone connects directly to a computer without additional equipment. An XLR microphone requires an audio interface or mixer; for one or two microphones, an audio interface is enough.

#### What is the best microphone for a beginner podcast?

For most beginners, a dynamic USB microphone is the best fit. It plugs directly into a computer and picks up less room noise than a condenser microphone. Widely used USB microphones cost about $100–$300. Models with an additional XLR connection let you add an audio interface later.

#### How much does podcast equipment cost?

You can start for $0 with a phone or computer you already own. A beginner setup with a USB microphone and closed-back headphones costs about $160–$500. An upgraded setup with an XLR microphone and audio interface costs about $320–$1,100.

For full budgets, see [how much it costs to start a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost).

#### Do I need a camera for a video podcast?

No additional camera is needed to start: you can use the camera on your phone or computer. The Substack Recording Studio supports recording with your camera on or audio only. A clip-on microphone keeps the microphone out of the picture.

## How to start a podcast for free

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/for-free

### Start a podcast with tools you already own

Use your existing equipment and free recording, editing, and hosting tools to publish your first episode.

Last updated: October 22, 2026 · By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack

### Can you start a podcast for free?

Yes. You can start with a phone or computer you already own, free recording and editing software, and a free podcast host. Hosts such as Substack store your episodes, create your RSS feed, and distribute your show to Apple Podcasts and Spotify at no cost. Listing on those platforms is also free.

This guide is part of the [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

#### Free podcast launch checklist

1. Choose a topic and plan your first episode.
2. Record with the microphone on your phone, computer, or earbuds.
3. Edit and export the episode with free software.
4. Make square cover art with a free design tool.
5. Set up your show on a free podcast host.
6. Publish your first episode.
7. Submit your show to Apple Podcasts and connect it to Spotify.

**An all-in-one option:** Substack lets you record, publish, and distribute a podcast with a free account, with no hosting fees or platform fees. Paid subscriptions have a separate revenue share, explained below.

### What do you need for a zero-budget podcast setup?

You need a phone or computer, a microphone—a built-in microphone or wired earbuds are enough to start—a quiet room, free recording and editing software, and a free podcast host.

| Item | Phone or computer setup | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Recording device | Your phone, laptop, or desktop | Already owned |
| Microphone | Built-in microphone or wired earbuds with a microphone | Already owned |
| Headphones | Any earbuds or headphones | Already owned |
| Recording software | Substack Recording Studio or another free tool | Free |
| Editing software | Free editing software | Free |
| Hosting and distribution | Free podcast host | Free on Substack |

**Optional upgrade:** A USB microphone costs about **$100–$300** and is the upgrade that makes the most difference to sound quality. See [podcast equipment for beginners](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/equipment).

Soft surfaces absorb sound and reduce echo. A small, furnished room usually sounds better than a large, empty one. Existing curtains, rugs, and upholstered furniture can help without extra spending.

### Choose a topic and plan your first episode

Pick a topic you could discuss every week without running out of things to say. Your first episode can be a conversation between friends, an interview, or a solo episode on one subject. It needs a reason for listeners to return, not necessarily a big idea.

Decide on your audience, show premise, first episode topic, and format:

| Planning decision | Example |
|---|---|
| Audience | First-time home gardeners in apartments |
| Show premise | Growing food on a balcony with no garden experience |
| First episode | “The five easiest vegetables to grow in containers, and the one to avoid” |
| Format | Solo, 20–30 minutes |

Before recording, write a short outline with an opening explaining the episode, the main points, and a closing telling listeners how to subscribe. You do not need a full script.

Related guides: [podcast ideas and topics](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-ideas) and [podcast script templates](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-script).

### Record your first episode with free tools

You can use Substack Recording Studio, a free remote-recording tool, or the voice recorder on your phone or computer.

#### Substack Recording Studio

The studio is free and built into Substack, allowing you to record and publish without extra software, exporting, or uploading. It supports:

- **Computer or phone recording**, including the Substack app.
- **Solo recording or up to two guests**, for three people total. Guests receive invitations by email, in the app, or in their browser.
- **Video or audio-only recording.** Audio-only mode uses the same tools without requiring you to appear on camera.
- **Screen sharing** with co-hosts during recording.
- **A logo or wordmark** added to the video.
- **Automatically created clips and thumbnails.** Substack creates short social-media clips and an adjustable thumbnail after recording.
- **Drafts for later publication.** Ending a recording creates a draft post that can be published immediately or later.

You can also go live on Substack from a computer or the app, with video or audio only, then publish the recording as an episode.

#### Free recording tools compared

| Tool | Free plan | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Substack Recording Studio | Free, built into Substack | Solo episodes and interviews with up to two remote guests, on a computer or phone |
| Phone voice recorder | Free; Voice Memos on iPhone or a voice recorder app on Android | Solo episodes |
| Audacity | Free, open-source software for Mac, Windows, and Linux | Solo episodes recorded on a computer |
| GarageBand | Free on Mac, iPhone, and iPad | Solo episodes on Apple devices |
| Descript | 60 minutes of media a month, including recordings; 720p video exports with a watermark | Remote interviews recorded and edited in one app |
| Riverside | Unlimited recording and editing; separate speaker tracks for the first 2 hours of recordings | Remote interviews, with each person's audio recorded on their own device |

**Free plans change often.** Check each tool's pricing page before relying on its limits.

To improve audio:

- Record a **30-second test** and listen back before every session.
- Keep the microphone about **one hand-width** from your mouth, at a constant distance.
- Ask remote guests to wear headphones so their speakers do not echo into their microphones.

See [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) for step-by-step guidance.

### Edit and export without paying for software

| Editor | Works on | Free plan | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audacity | Mac, Windows, Linux | Fully free, open source | Records and edits on a computer |
| GarageBand | Mac, iPhone, iPad | Fully free | Comes installed on most Apple devices |
| Descript | Mac, Windows, web | About 1 hour of media per month; video exports carry a watermark | Edit audio by editing its transcript like a text document |

For a first episode, focus on these essential edits:

1. **Cut** long pauses, false starts, and off-topic sections.
2. **Adjust volume** so every voice is at the same level.
3. **Export** as an MP3 file.
4. **Listen** to the entire exported file on headphones.

Listeners expect natural conversation, so you do not need to remove every small mistake.

On Substack, upload the exported file as a new episode. For video episodes, Substack creates a transcript automatically; you can also upload a separately edited audio version for podcast-app listeners.

See [how to edit a podcast with free software](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/editing) for more cleanup guidance.

### Create artwork and publish your show

#### Make free cover art

Podcast apps require square cover art. Apple Podcasts requires:

- At least **1400 × 1400 pixels**, and at most **3000 × 3000 pixels**.
- A **JPEG or PNG** file.

Free design tools such as Canva offer podcast templates at these sizes. Keep the title large because most listeners see the cover as a small thumbnail. See [podcast cover art templates](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cover-art).

#### Hosting and listing are different steps

- **Hosting** stores episodes and creates your RSS feed—the link podcast apps use to find your show. You need a host before listing your show in apps.
- **Listing** means submitting that feed to apps such as Apple Podcasts and Spotify so listeners can find it. Listing is free.

Learn more about [creating a podcast RSS feed](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed), or compare plan features and limits in [the best free podcast hosting platforms](https://substack.com/best-free-podcast-hosting).

#### Publish on Substack for free

1. Go to [Substack](https://substack.com), select **Start your Substack**, create a free account, and name your publication. You can use your podcast's name or your own.
2. Open your **Dashboard** from the top-right corner of your publication's page.
3. Select **Podcast → Start your podcast → Create a new podcast → Next**.
4. Add your cover art, title, description, language, and categories, then select **Create podcast**.
5. Publish your first episode. Each episode also goes to subscribers by email and appears in the Substack app.
6. In podcast settings, select **Connect to Spotify**.
7. Copy your RSS feed URL from podcast settings and submit it to Apple Podcasts and other podcast apps.

**You must publish at least one episode before podcast apps accept the feed.** If a full episode is not ready, publish a short trailer introducing the show.

Substack hosts audio and video podcasts with no hosting fees or platform fees. You own your subscriber list: you receive subscribers' email addresses and can export the list at any time.

### When does a free podcast start costing money?

A podcast can remain free as long as you want. Costs arise when you choose upgraded equipment, paid software, or help with editing or artwork.

| Item | Free option | When it can cost money |
|---|---|---|
| Hosting and distribution | Free on Substack, with no hosting fees or platform fees | Some other hosts charge monthly fees or limit free storage |
| Apple Podcasts and Spotify listings | Free | Never, for a free show |
| Recording | Substack Recording Studio, phone, Audacity, GarageBand | When you exceed a tool's free limits, such as Descript's 60 minutes of media a month |
| Editing | Audacity, GarageBand, Descript free plan | When you exceed a free plan's monthly limit |
| Equipment | What you already own | USB microphone: about $100–$300; closed-back headphones: about $60–$200 |
| Cover art | Free design templates | When you hire a designer |

#### What if you earn money from your podcast?

Substack is free to use for free or paid podcasts. **If you enable paid subscriptions, you keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees.**

For example:

- **100 subscribers at $5/month:** $500 in monthly revenue; you keep $450, minus credit card fees.
- **500 subscribers at $5/month:** you keep $2,250 a month under that revenue share.

See [making money from a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/make-money).

You can [restrict episodes to paying subscribers](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast). Other listeners hear a short preview and see a subscription offer. The page's example paywalled episode also offers a free trial.

Paying subscribers can listen in the Substack app, on Spotify, or in other podcast apps through a private RSS feed. See [podcast startup and recurring costs](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost) for a fuller breakdown.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Is Substack free for podcasts?

Yes. Substack hosts audio and video podcasts for free and distributes them to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other podcast apps. If you enable paid subscriptions, you keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees.

#### Can I start a podcast on my phone for free?

Yes. Record with the phone's built-in microphone using the Substack app or a free voice recorder, then publish through a free host such as Substack.

#### Does it cost money to be on Spotify or Apple Podcasts?

No. Listing is free, but you need a podcast host first. That host can also be free.

#### What is the best free podcast hosting?

It depends on your needs. Check storage and episode limits, distribution to Apple Podcasts and Spotify, video support, access to listeners' email addresses, and monetization options. The page states that Substack includes all of these on its free plan. See the [free podcast hosting comparison](https://substack.com/best-free-podcast-hosting).

#### How long does it take to start a podcast for free?

You can publish a first episode in a day: a few hours to plan and record, an hour or two to edit, and a few minutes to set up a free host. Apple Podcasts and Spotify can take **a few hours to a few days** to list a new show.

## How to grow a podcast audience

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience

### How do you grow a podcast audience?

To grow a podcast audience, publish on a reliable schedule and turn listeners into subscribers. Share clips of every episode and work with other creators who reach the same people. Every new subscriber hears your future episodes, so growth builds on itself.

On Substack, these tools are built in and free. Episodes can go to subscribers’ inboxes and the Substack app, Substack makes clips from videos, and other creators can recommend your show. Hosting is free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees. Existing shows can [move to Substack](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/move-your-podcast).

The main ways to grow a podcast are:

1. Make a show people want to follow.
2. Turn listeners into subscribers.
3. Share clips of every episode.
4. Work with other creators.
5. Get Recommendations from other creators.
6. Share episodes and clips on Notes.
7. Help people find episodes in search and podcast apps.
8. Build a community around your show.
9. Measure what brings in new listeners.

This guide is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### Make a show people want to follow

People subscribe when they know what a show is for and when the next episode arrives. Before promoting your podcast, check three things:

- **A clear promise.** One sentence should explain who the show is for and what listeners get. See [podcast ideas and topics](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-ideas).
- **A name and cover art that work at a small size.** Most people first see a show as a small square in an app. See [podcast name ideas](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-names) and [podcast cover art](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cover-art).
- **A reliable publishing schedule.** Reliability matters more than frequency. Listeners who know when to expect you come back.

A single strong episode can bring in many new subscribers. [Prof G Media](https://www.profgmedia.com/)’s two biggest subscriber drivers in its first weeks were [an interview with James Talarico and a deep dive on storytelling](https://on.substack.com/p/scott-galloway-had-the-audience-heres). At the time, it was adding about 150 paid subscribers a week, and many more free ones.

### How do you turn listeners into subscribers?

A subscriber hears every new episode without having to look for it. Ask for the subscription in every episode and explain what subscribers get.

- **Ask at the start and end.** One sentence is enough: where to subscribe and what is coming next week.
- **Send every episode to subscribers.** When publishing on Substack, select **Send via email and the Substack app**. Subscribers receive it in their inbox and the app, as well as their podcast app.
- **Reach listeners in the Substack app.** Its podcast tab lets existing listeners find new episodes and new listeners discover your show.

If you already have a newsletter, start there. When Shea Serrano launched [Organizing Things](https://goodmovie.substack.com/podcast) with Jason Concepcion, his newsletter, GOOD MOVIE, already had 128,000 free subscribers. In its first week, the show reached [126,000 views and 10,385 downloads with no paid promotion](https://on.substack.com/p/shea-serrano-podcast). Its free first episode and short free previews of later episodes help new listeners find it.

### How do you use clips to grow a podcast?

Clips are short episode highlights that people can watch and share on social media. They show new people what your show is like before they play a full episode.

Substack includes:

- **Automatic clips.** When you record, upload, or livestream a video, Substack makes portrait and landscape clips. Select the scissors icon in the video editor to see them, or make your own clip of up to five minutes.
- **Sharing.** Share clips as Substack Notes or to Instagram Stories and Reels from the Substack app. You can also upload them to LinkedIn or download them as MP4 files.
- **YouTube Shorts.** Connect your YouTube account under **Connected accounts** in publication settings, then choose automatic clips to post as Shorts.

Clips made on Substack had brought in [nearly 500,000 free subscriptions](https://on.substack.com/p/new-livestreaming-from-desktop) by December 2025. Organizing Things makes clipping a habit: its editor cuts two social clips from each episode. For recording on camera, see [how to start a video podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast).

### How do you grow by working with other creators?

Guests and collaborators bring their own listeners. When a guest shares an episode, their audience hears your show.

- **Invite guests with their own audiences.** The free [Substack Recording Studio](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) supports recording with up to two guests, each joining from a computer or the Substack app.
- **Appear on other shows.** Guest appearances reach listeners who already like podcasts on your topic.
- **Go live together.** Up to three people can stream together in a Substack livestream. Each co-host can join from a computer or the app.
- **Find partners with Creator Match.** [Creator Match](https://on.substack.com/p/new-on-substack-creator-match-audience) finds creators with similar audience sizes and interests, ranking them by how well a collaboration could work for both parties. Every publisher has access through their dashboard at `your.substack.com/publish/creator-matches` and can message other creators directly.

### How do Recommendations help a podcast grow?

Substack creators recommend one another’s publications to their subscribers. When someone subscribes to a show that recommends yours, they see your show and can subscribe too.

To recommend a show:

1. Select **Recommendations**, then **Add Recommendation**, in your Substack navigation bar.
2. Search for the publication and add a short blurb explaining why you recommend it.

Recommendations appear in three places:

- After someone subscribes to your show.
- On your publication’s homepage.
- In Recommendation digest emails to your subscribers.

Creators you recommend receive an email and are prompted to recommend you back. Your **Recommendations** tab shows who recommends you and how many free subscriptions each Recommendation brought in.

### How do Notes help a podcast grow?

Notes is Substack’s short-form feed for updates, clips, and links. People who do not yet subscribe to your show can see your Notes, giving new listeners another way to find you.

- **Post every episode as a Note.** [Split Zone Duo](https://www.splitzoneduo.com/) publishes its episodes as Notes posts. Host Richard Johnson [calls Notes the show’s best and most direct connection](https://on.substack.com/p/three-models-for-building-community) to what it does.
- **Share clips before and after each episode.** A pre-release clip acts as a teaser; a later clip sends viewers to the full episode. [Sharing clips to Notes](https://on.substack.com/p/substack-video-clipper-and-production-tools) introduces your show to people who have not heard it.

### How do people find podcast episodes in search and apps?

Listeners search podcast apps and the web for topics and guests. Describe each episode using words they would search for.

- **Write a descriptive title.** Name the guest or topic, rather than using only an episode number.
- **Add show notes.** Notes entered in Substack’s podcast editor become the episode description in Apple Podcasts and Spotify.
- **Show the transcript.** Every Substack podcast episode gets an AI-generated transcript on its web page. Listeners can read along and click text to jump to that part of the episode. You can edit the transcript or upload a `.txt`, `.srt`, or `.vtt` file.
- **Get your show into every app.** See [how to get your podcast on Spotify](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/spotify), [how to get your podcast on Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts), and [what a podcast RSS feed is](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### How do you build a community around your podcast?

A community gives listeners a reason to return between episodes. Substack Chat is built in on the web and in the app.

- **Start a subscriber chat.** Select **Chat** in your dashboard, then **+New**, and choose who can join and reply.
- **Use channels.** Create up to 16 chat channels, each with its own name and audience. For example, run a paid-only chat alongside a free main chat.
- **Send a thread by email.** Turn on **Send as email** to deliver a chat thread to subscribers’ inboxes too.

Examples include:

- [Drop Your Buffs](https://dropyourbuffs.substack.com/), from Sean Ross and Evan Ross Katz, holds live watch parties in its paid-subscriber chat for each *Survivor* episode. Sean Ross says listeners outside the chat [get only half the story](https://on.substack.com/p/the-tribe-has-spoken-how-drop-your).
- College football podcast [Split Zone Duo](https://www.splitzoneduo.com/) [opens live chat on game days](https://on.substack.com/p/three-models-for-building-community) to talk with listeners during games.
- Fashion and culture podcast [Nymphet Alumni](https://substack.com/@nymphetalumni) has a subscriber chat. Host Biz Sherbert says its community is [now self-sustaining](https://on.substack.com/p/three-models-for-building-community), with listeners organizing their own meetups.

When your community is ready to support you, you can turn on paid subscriptions. You keep 90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees. See [how to start a paid podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast).

### How do you measure podcast growth?

Track which episodes bring in new subscribers, then make more episodes like them. Substack’s **Podcast** tab shows:

- Average downloads 7, 30, and 90 days after each episode is published.
- Daily and total downloads, and downloads for each episode.
- Listeners’ countries and podcast apps.

Each episode also has a post in the **Posts** tab, showing views, email open rates, and subscriptions gained after people listened.

Substack’s podcast download measurement is [certified by IAB Tech Lab](https://support.substack.com/hc/en-us/articles/20501349089300-Are-Substack-podcast-analytics-IAB-certified). An IAB-certified download counts at least 60 seconds of an episode downloaded to a unique device in a 24-hour period. This provides industry-standard numbers for pitching sponsors and reporting show performance.

Substack’s [podcast sponsorships](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships) provide another way to earn as an audience grows. Dynamic sponsorships, described as being in early access, let creators run campaigns with their own sponsors and update ads across their back catalog without re-editing episodes. Participation is optional, and creators choose which kinds of sponsors to work with. See [how to make money podcasting](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/make-money) for other earning options.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is the best way to grow a podcast?

Combine methods rather than relying on one: ask listeners to subscribe, share clips of every episode, invite guests with their own audiences, and recommend creators who can recommend you back. Substack says these tools are built in and free.

#### How do you promote a podcast?

Share episode clips on social media and Notes, appear as a guest on other shows, and ask listeners to share episodes. Make marketing part of every episode, not just the launch.

#### How do you get podcast listeners for free?

Use free channels such as social media clips, YouTube Shorts, guest appearances, and Recommendations from other creators. Substack hosting has no hosting or platform fees, and episodes can reach subscribers through email and the Substack app.

#### Do clips help grow a podcast?

Yes. Clips made on Substack had brought in nearly 500,000 free subscriptions by December 2025. Substack automatically makes clips from videos, which can be shared to Notes, Instagram, LinkedIn, and YouTube Shorts.

#### How do I know if my podcast is growing?

Watch downloads and the subscribers each episode brings in. Substack’s Podcast tab shows average downloads 7, 30, and 90 days after each episode, while each episode’s post shows subscriptions gained.

## How to make money podcasting

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/make-money

### How podcasts make money

Podcasts earn money in three main ways: paid subscriptions, sponsorships and ads, and products, events, or services sold to listeners. Paid subscriptions let listeners pay directly each month, so income does not depend on download numbers.

On Substack, podcast hosting is always free, with no hosting fees or platform fees. When paid subscriptions are enabled, creators keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees. Creators publishing podcasts on Substack collectively earn [over $200 million a year](https://podnews.net/update/substack-podcast-tab).

*Last updated: October 27, 2026. By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack.*

| Way to earn | How it works | Works best when |
|---|---|---|
| Paid subscriptions | Listeners pay monthly or yearly for bonus, ad-free, or early episodes | Listeners want more of your show |
| Sponsorships and advertising | Brands pay to reach listeners in ad breaks | You have a clearly defined audience brands want to reach |
| Products, events, and services | Sell merchandise, live shows, courses, or your expertise | You can create and deliver offerings that fit your show |

This page is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### How paid podcast subscriptions work

Listeners pay a monthly or yearly price for episodes and extras that free listeners do not receive. Common benefits include:

- **Bonus episodes** available only to paying subscribers.
- **Ad-free versions** of every episode.
- **Early access** to new episodes.
- **The full archive**, while free listeners receive recent episodes.
- **Livestreams and chat** with the hosts, which can be organized into community channels on Substack.

Examples include:

- **[Prof G Media](https://www.profgmedia.com/):** Scott Galloway’s podcasts moved to Substack in March 2026. Prof G+ members get ad-free versions of The Prof G Pod, Prof G Markets, Raging Moderates, and China Decode.
- **[The Bulwark](https://www.thebulwark.com/bulwark-plus):** Bulwark+ members get ad-free episodes of every Bulwark show, member-only episodes, and a private podcast feed for any podcast app.
- **[Organizing Things](https://goodmovie.substack.com/podcast):** Shea Serrano and Jason Concepcion keep the first episode free. Later episodes have short public previews, while paid subscribers hear the full episodes.

#### How to turn on paid subscriptions on Substack

1. In your publication’s settings, open **Payments**, then create and connect a Stripe account. Stripe pays earnings into your bank account.
2. Set monthly and yearly prices. You can also add a higher-priced founding member plan for listeners who want to pay more.
3. When publishing an episode, select **Everyone** for a free episode or **Paid subscribers only** for a paid episode.
4. To provide a sample, upload or record a short preview. Free subscribers hear the preview and then see an offer to subscribe.

The page illustrates this with Skyline Trails, a sample podcast from Substack’s Help Center: a paid episode displays a short preview, a seven-day free trial offer, and a list of subscription benefits.

Paying subscribers can listen in the Substack app or on [Spotify](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/spotify) after linking their Substack account. In [Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts) and other podcast apps, they use a [private RSS feed](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed). See [how to start a paid podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast) for the full setup.

### How podcast sponsorships work

Sponsors pay to reach listeners through host-read ads or ads inserted into breaks. They look for steady downloads and a clear audience, so reliable download numbers help sell ads. Substack’s podcast download measurement is certified by IAB Tech Lab, the industry standard for counting downloads.

Substack offers two approaches:

- **Sponsored free episodes — available now:** Upload a separate version for free subscribers and mark it as sponsored. Paid subscribers receive the full episode without ads, while free subscribers receive the sponsored version.
- **Dynamic ad insertion — in early access:** Substack announced podcast sponsorships on October 21, 2026. Creators can run campaigns with their own sponsors and update ads across their back catalog without re-editing episodes.

Third-party sponsorship marketplaces are described as coming soon, allowing creators to fill marked ad breaks. Creators decide how many ads run and which kinds of sponsors they accept. See the [podcast sponsorships announcement and early-access information](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships).

Prof G Media combines sponsorships and subscriptions: its podcasts carry ads, while paying listeners can choose an ad-free version.

### Other ways a podcast can make money

**Platform ad programs.** For video episodes published on YouTube, the YouTube Partner Program can share ad revenue. A channel needs 1,000 subscribers, plus either:

- 4,000 public watch hours in the last 12 months; or
- 10 million Shorts views in the last 90 days.

See [how to start a video podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast).

**Products, events, and services.** Merchandise, live shows, courses, books, and consulting build on the trust a show earns and can also grow subscriptions. [Blocked and Reported](https://www.blockedandreported.org/), with Katie Herzog and Jesse Singal, has sold mugs, tote bags, and shirts through its merchandise store.

### How much podcasters make

Podcast income depends on how many listeners pay directly or how many downloads sponsors pay for. The page gives these subscription examples:

| Paying subscribers | Monthly price | Monthly revenue | Creator’s share after Substack’s 10%, before credit card fees |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | $5 | $500 | $450 |
| 500 | $5 | $2,500 | $2,250 |

Examples from shows on Substack illustrate the range:

- Creators publishing podcasts on Substack collectively earn over $200 million a year, according to [Podnews](https://podnews.net/update/substack-podcast-tab).
- [Prof G Media](https://www.profgmedia.com/) earns [about $20 million a year from its podcasts](https://on.substack.com/p/scott-galloway-had-the-audience-heres). In May 2026, it was adding about 150 paid subscribers per week on Substack.
- [Organizing Things](https://goodmovie.substack.com/podcast) reached [10,385 downloads with no paid promotion](https://on.substack.com/p/shea-serrano-podcast) in its first week, and its launch brought about 120 new paid subscribers.

For operating expenses, see [how much it costs to start a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost).

### How to start making money from a podcast

1. **Build a free audience first.** Publish free episodes on a reliable schedule. Episodes can be recorded in the free [Substack Recording Studio](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording). See [how to grow a podcast audience](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience) for ways to reach more listeners.
2. **Decide what paying listeners get.** Choose one or two extras you can deliver every week, such as bonus or ad-free episodes.
3. **Turn on paid subscriptions.** Create and connect a Stripe account, set prices, and mark each episode as free or paid.
4. **Offer products or events to engaged listeners.** Merchandise and live shows can be profitable additions to subscriptions once listeners know and trust you.

For free tools at each step, see [how to start a podcast for free](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/for-free).

Substack supports free and paid episodes within one show, with distribution to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and subscribers’ inboxes.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can you make money from a podcast with a small audience?

Yes. Paid subscriptions do not depend on large download numbers. At $5 per month, 100 paying subscribers generate $500 monthly, with $450 retained before credit card fees. With 500 subscribers, revenue is $2,500 monthly, with $2,250 retained before credit card fees.

#### Does it cost anything to make money from a podcast on Substack?

Substack hosts and distributes podcasts for free, with no hosting fees or platform fees. When paid subscriptions are enabled, creators keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees. An existing show can [move to Substack](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/move-your-podcast) for free.

#### Do you need sponsors to make money podcasting?

No. Paid subscriptions allow listeners to pay directly, with or without sponsors. On Substack, paying subscribers can receive an ad-free episode while free listeners receive a sponsored version.

#### How do podcasters get paid?

Sponsors usually pay a rate per thousand downloads, called **CPM**, or a flat fee per episode. Paid subscribers pay monthly or yearly regardless of download numbers. On Substack, subscription payments go to the creator’s Stripe account, which pays out to their bank account.

## How to move your podcast to Substack

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/move-your-podcast

### Moving your podcast to Substack

Bring your episodes, listeners, and subscribers to Substack, where hosting is free and episodes also reach subscribers’ inboxes.

Last updated: October 27, 2026. By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack.

To move your podcast, import your episodes using your current RSS feed URL, then ask your previous host to redirect the old feed to your new Substack feed. Followers in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other apps continue receiving episodes without taking action.

The process is:

1. Import your episodes.
2. Check your show details.
3. Redirect your old feed to Substack.
4. Check Apple Podcasts and Spotify.
5. Bring your email list and paid subscribers.
6. Tell listeners about the move.

This guide is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### What happens when you move a podcast to Substack?

Moving, migrating, or transferring a podcast means switching hosts—the service that stores your audio and creates your RSS feed. When you import your podcast, Substack becomes your host and creates a new feed.

According to Apple, a redirect from your old host moves all followers to the new feed, including listeners outside Apple Podcasts. Downloaded episodes stay downloaded, and followers retain their place in each episode.

Substack provides:

- **Free hosting:** no hosting fees or platform fees.
- **Email delivery:** episodes reach subscribers’ inboxes and the Substack app, as well as podcast apps.
- **Paid subscriptions:** you keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees.
- **Free Substack Recording Studio:** record with up to two guests. See [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) and [how to start a video podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast).
- **Industry-standard download statistics:** certified by IAB Tech Lab and shareable with sponsors.

Substack is also adding [podcast sponsorships](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships). Dynamic sponsorships, in early access, let you run campaigns with your own sponsors and update ads across your back catalog without re-editing episodes. Third-party sponsorship marketplaces that fill marked ad breaks are coming soon. Participation is optional; you control ad volume and acceptable sponsor types.

### How to import your podcast to Substack

Copy your current RSS feed URL from your existing host, then:

1. In your Substack dashboard, select **Podcast** in the left column, then **Create podcast**.
2. Select **Import an existing podcast** rather than **Create a new podcast**.
3. Paste your current RSS feed URL and select **Submit**.
4. Review the imported episodes and select **Import all episodes**.

Imported episodes appear in your **Posts** list.

If you already have a podcast section on Substack, open your publication’s **Settings → Sections**, select the three dots next to the section, then **Edit → Import podcast**.

**After importing, publish new episodes on Substack.** Episodes added at your old host will not appear on Substack.

#### What to check after importing

- **Show details:** check your title, description, categories, and artwork in **Settings → Podcasts → Edit** next to your podcast, under **Basics**. These settings supply the details shown in podcast apps. For sizes, see [podcast cover art](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cover-art).
- **Episodes:** check the Posts list to confirm every episode arrived with its title and description.
- **Paid episodes:** if you plan to offer bonus or ad-free episodes, see [how to start a paid podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast).

### How to redirect your old podcast RSS feed to Substack

A **301 permanent redirect** from your old RSS feed to your Substack feed preserves existing followers across podcast apps.

1. **Copy your Substack feed.** Open **Settings → Podcasts → Edit** next to your podcast. Scroll to **Distribute your podcast** and select **Copy URL** in the Apple Podcasts section.
2. **Set up the redirect at your previous host.** Paste your Substack feed URL into that host’s redirect setting. Apple notes that most hosting providers can set this up for you.
3. **Keep the redirect in place.** Apple recommends at least **four weeks**, so followers pick up the latest episodes from the new feed.

#### Redirect settings at common hosts

| Moving from | Where to set the redirect | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spotify for Creators | On the web, open **Settings → Redirect your podcast**, paste your Substack feed, and select **Redirect**. | Not available in the mobile app. Turn off Subscriptions first. The redirect can take up to **7 days**. |
| Buzzsprout | Open **Settings → Podcast Settings → Redirect**. Check the box and select **Redirect RSS Feed and Downgrade to the Buzzsprout Free Plan**. | Redirect each podcast separately. Buzzsprout recommends keeping your account for at least **three weeks**. |
| Libsyn | Open **Settings → Redirects**, enter your Substack feed, select **Save**, then **Yes**. | Import episodes first. The redirect remains even if you close your account. |
| Podbean | Open **Settings → Feed → Advanced Feed Settings**. Enter your Substack feed in **Redirect to a New Feed**, then select **Update Options**. | Clear that field to remove the redirect. |
| Acast | Open **Show Settings → Show redirection**. Check the confirmation box, select **Redirect Feed**, and paste your Substack feed. | Export listening and revenue data first. If you use Acast ads, contact Acast support before redirecting. |
| RSS.com | Open **Settings → Redirect My Podcast → Redirect my show**, paste your Substack feed, and select **Move My Show**. | Turn off Copy Protection first. Redirects work on every plan, including Free. |
| Captivate | Open **Podcast Settings → Cancel Show**, choose the Moving option, enter your Substack feed, and select **Move Podcast**. | Import episodes first. Download analytics and remove dynamic ads before moving. |
| Transistor | Open **Settings**, find the RSS Feed section, paste your Substack feed into **Permanent Redirect (301)**, and save. | The redirect is free and remains even if you cancel your account. |
| Patreon, for paid members | Move paid members rather than a feed. Select **Audience → CSV** to export your member list, then import it to Substack. | Some emails may be missing if members chose not to share them. Follow the paid-subscriber steps below. |

For background, see [what a podcast RSS feed is](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### How to update Apple Podcasts and Spotify after moving

With a redirect in place, followers in Apple Podcasts and Spotify continue receiving new episodes from your Substack feed.

- **Apple Podcasts:** no change is needed in Apple Podcasts Connect. If you can no longer access your old feed to redirect it, sign in to Apple Podcasts Connect, select your show, select **Edit** next to the RSS feed URL, enter your Substack feed URL, and select **Save**. Paste your Apple Podcasts link into your Substack podcast settings so a **Listen on Apple** link appears on episodes.
- **Spotify:** Spotify says a redirect keeps listeners receiving new episodes. If it asks you to verify ownership, it sends a code to the email address in your Substack RSS feed. To receive it, open **Settings → Community** and set **Who can reply to your emails** to **Everyone**. You can also change **Email address for RSS feeds** in the **Details** section.

For paid episodes on Spotify, see [how to get your podcast on Spotify](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/spotify). For Apple distribution, see [how to get your podcast on Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts).

### How to bring your email list and paid subscribers to Substack

You can import your email list and give paying supporters complimentary access while they subscribe again on Substack.

#### Import your email list

1. In your dashboard, select **Subscribers → Add subscribers**.
2. Under **Add subscribers by upload**, upload a **.csv, .xlsx, or .ods** file containing subscriber email addresses.
3. Confirm that subscribers opted in to receive your emails, then select **Import**.

Substack skips duplicate email addresses. It suggests not sending a welcome email during import, so you can announce the move when your publication is ready.

#### Bring over paid subscribers

**Payment details cannot move between platforms.** Paying supporters must subscribe again on Substack. To preserve access in the meantime:

1. **Export your lists.** Download your email and paid-subscriber lists, including each paid member’s renewal or expiration date.
2. **Create and connect a Stripe account.** Open **Settings → Payments → Connect with Stripe**, create your Stripe account, and set up paid plans.
3. **Import members and grant paid members complimentary subscriptions.** On the Subscribers page under **All Subscribers**, select the relevant members, select the three dots, then **Comp**. Available durations are **7 days, 30 days, 90 days, 6 months, 1 year, or forever**.
4. **Pause billing on your current platform.**
5. **Publish a free post explaining the move.** Explain why you moved and include a **Subscribe** button so paid members can start a Substack subscription. Substack sends reminders as complimentary subscriptions end.

For other revenue options, see [how to make money podcasting](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/make-money).

### How to tell listeners about the move

The redirect moves followers in podcast apps. To bring listeners to your Substack as well:

- Mention the move at the start or end of upcoming episodes.
- Add a link to your Substack in show notes.
- Post about it on social media.

See [how to grow a podcast audience](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience) for more audience-building guidance.

### Which podcasts have moved to Substack?

- [Prof G Media](https://www.profgmedia.com/), Scott Galloway’s company, brought its newsletters and podcasts together on Substack in **March 2026**. Prof G+ members receive ad-free podcast versions, a paid option listeners had requested.
- [Blocked and Reported](https://www.blockedandreported.org/p/why-blocked-and-reported-moved-to), with Katie Herzog and Jesse Singal, moved its entire operation from Patreon to Substack.
- [The Fifth Column](https://www.wethefifth.com/) and [American Prestige](https://americanprestige.substack.com/) also moved from Patreon to Substack.

### What if you want to keep your current host?

You can add your podcast to Substack without moving its hosting. Substack reads your existing RSS feed and publishes new episodes automatically. Audio, ads, and analytics remain with your existing host, and dynamic ads continue running.

1. In your Substack dashboard, select **Podcast → I have a podcast hosted elsewhere → Save**.
2. Select **Distribute to Substack** and paste your RSS feed URL.
3. Review the show details populated from the feed and select **Continue**.
4. Choose whether to publish new episodes automatically and whether to import your back catalog.

When you are ready to move hosting, follow the import and redirect steps above.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Will you lose listeners if you switch podcast hosts?

No, provided your previous host redirects the old feed to your Substack feed. Followers in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other apps move to the new feed, and downloaded episodes remain downloaded.

#### How do I move from Spotify for Creators to Substack?

Import your show using its Spotify for Creators RSS feed. Turn off Spotify for Creators Subscriptions if you use them. On the web, open **Settings → Redirect your podcast**, paste your Substack feed, and select **Redirect**. It can take up to **7 days**.

#### Does moving a podcast to Substack cost anything?

No. Hosting and distribution are free, with no hosting fees or platform fees. If you enable paid subscriptions, you keep **90%** of earnings, minus credit card fees.

#### Can I move paid subscribers to Substack?

Yes. Import their email addresses, grant complimentary access for time already paid for, and ask them to subscribe on Substack. Payment details cannot transfer, so each paying subscriber signs up again.

#### How long should I keep the redirect from my old host?

Apple recommends at least **four weeks**. Apps retrieve the new feed on their own schedules; Spotify says a redirect can take up to **7 days** to complete.

#### Can I keep my current host and still use Substack?

Yes. Select **Podcast → I have a podcast hosted elsewhere → Distribute to Substack**. Substack publishes episodes from your existing feed while your audio, ads, and analytics remain with your current host.

## How to start a paid podcast

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast

### How do you start a paid podcast?

To start a paid podcast, decide what paying listeners get, set your prices, and turn on paid subscriptions with your podcast host. Publish some episodes for paid subscribers only, who can hear them through a private feed in their podcast app.

On Substack, hosting is free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees. Free and paid episodes are part of the same show. When you turn on paid subscriptions, you keep 90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees.

The main steps are:

1. Choose what paying listeners get.
2. Set your prices.
3. Turn on paid subscriptions and publish paid episodes.
4. Add free previews to paid episodes.
5. Deliver paid episodes through the Substack app, Apple Podcasts, and Spotify.
6. Turn free listeners into paying subscribers.

This page is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

*Last updated: October 27, 2026. By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack.*

### What is a paid podcast?

A paid podcast, also called a subscription podcast or premium podcast, is a show where listeners pay a subscription to hear some or all episodes. It can be fully paid, or keep a free show and charge for extras.

#### Choose a paid podcast model

| Model | What paying listeners get | Good fit for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bonus episodes | Extra episodes on top of a free show | Shows that already have free listeners |
| Free previews | The full episode, while free listeners hear part of it | Shows whose episodes hook listeners in the first few minutes |
| Ad-free episodes | The same episodes without ads | Shows that run ads or sponsorships |
| Early access | New episodes before everyone else | Shows that publish on a regular schedule |
| Paid archive | Older episodes beyond the free ones | Shows with a long back catalog |
| All episodes paid | Every episode, with little or nothing free | Shows whose audience already pays, such as readers of a paid newsletter |

Examples of these models on Substack include:

- **[Prof G Media](https://www.profgmedia.com/about):** Scott Galloway’s company gives Prof G+ members ad-free versions of its shows, including *The Prof G Pod* and *Prof G Markets*.
- **[The Fifth Column](https://www.wethefifth.com/about):** Kmele Foster, Michael Moynihan, and Matt Welch keep the main show free and ad-free in podcast apps. Paid subscribers also get a weekly bonus episode, live events, and Zoom calls.
- **[Serious Trouble](https://www.serioustrouble.show/about):** Josh Barro and Ken White give free subscribers at least 20 episodes a year; paid subscribers get every episode.

### How much should you charge for a paid podcast?

On Substack, you set a monthly and an annual price. You can also add a founding member plan for listeners who want to pay more. For accounts paid in US dollars, the minimum is **$5 a month and $30 a year**. Serious Trouble charges $6 a month or $60 a year.

- **Monthly and annual plans:** Substack does not offer a yearly-only plan, so you must set both. An annual price below the cost of 12 monthly payments gives listeners a reason to commit for a year.
- **Founding member plan:** Listeners choose to pay any amount above your monthly and annual prices. On The Fifth Column, founding members get a monthly live listen-in on a recording.
- **Changing prices later:** New subscribers pay the new price; existing subscribers stay on the plan they paid for.

#### What a paid podcast costs on Substack

Substack hosts your podcast for free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees. When you turn on paid subscriptions, you keep 90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees. Payments go through your own Stripe account.

You can also sell subscriptions inside Apple Podcasts through the Apple Podcasters Program, which charges an annual fee. Substack subscribers can still listen in Apple Podcasts through a private feed.

| | Substack | Apple Podcasters Program |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Annual fee | $0 | $19.99 in the US |
| What you keep | 90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees | 70% of the subscription price in a subscriber’s first year, then 85%, minus applicable taxes |
| Where paying listeners hear paid episodes | The Substack app, Apple Podcasts and other apps through a private feed, and Spotify | Apple Podcasts |

For broader startup expenses, see [how much it costs to start a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost).

### How to set up a paid podcast on Substack

Create and connect a Stripe account, set your prices, and publish episodes for paid subscribers. Free and paid episodes remain part of the same show.

1. **Create and connect a Stripe account.** In your Substack’s **Settings**, select **Payments**, then **Connect with Stripe**. Create your Stripe account on Stripe’s website, including a bank account for payouts.
2. **Set your prices and turn on payments.** Back in **Settings**, set prices for monthly, yearly, and founding member plans. Turn on **Enable payments**. Listeners cannot see paid options until you do.
3. **Create an episode.** From your dashboard, select **Create → Podcast**, then **Record** or **Select file**.
4. **Choose who can hear it.** Select **Continue**. On the Publish page, set the audience to **Paid subscribers only** for a paid episode or **Everyone** for a free episode.
5. **Publish.** Send the episode by email and to the Substack app, or publish it on the web only.

You can also connect Stripe in the Substack app: tap **Settings → Payments → Connect Stripe**.
