For related guidance, see [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) for free browser recording, or [how to start a video podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast).

### How to add a free preview to a paid episode

A free preview lets free listeners hear part of a paid episode before deciding whether to subscribe. Paid subscribers hear the full episode.

To add a preview:

1. Create the paid episode and select the **Preview** icon in the podcast editor.
2. Upload or record a separate audio file for free listeners, or choose part of the paid audio to offer for free.
3. Leave **Free version is sponsored** unchecked, set the audience to **Paid subscribers only**, and check **Send via email and the Substack app**.

Free listeners hear the preview in the Substack app, on the web, and in podcast apps, then see an offer to subscribe. The page illustrates this with a paid episode of the example podcast *Skyline Trails*, showing a Preview label and an explanation of what a subscription includes.

The same editor can create an **ad-free version for paid subscribers**. Check **Free version is sponsored** and set the audience to **Everyone**. Free listeners hear the sponsored version; paid subscribers hear the full episode without ads.

### How do paying subscribers listen to paid episodes?

Paying subscribers can listen in the Substack app, in [Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts) and other podcast apps through a private feed, and on [Spotify](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/spotify).

- **Substack app and web:** Paid episodes play for paid subscribers wherever they open your publication.
- **Apple Podcasts and other apps:** Every subscriber gets a unique private RSS feed. A paid subscriber’s feed includes paid episodes. To add it, subscribers open the publication’s **Manage subscription** page, find **Private podcast feed**, select **Set up podcast**, and copy the feed address. In Apple Podcasts, they go to **Library**, tap the three dots, and select **Add a Show by URL**.
- **Spotify:** Select **Connect to Spotify** in your podcast settings to send free and paid episodes to Spotify. Paid episodes show a padlock. Paid subscribers select **Get access** and link their Substack account; free listeners who link their accounts are invited to upgrade. Settings can show separate Spotify links for paid and free subscribers.

**Limitations:** Spotify does not play free previews or founding member episodes. If a subscriber cancels, their private feed returns to your free episodes.

For more detail, see [what a podcast RSS feed is](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### How to turn free listeners into paying subscribers

Keep your main show free and easy to find, and show listeners what they are missing.

- **Keep the main show free in every app.** Free episodes on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and other apps help [new listeners find you](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience).
- **Add free previews to paid episodes.** Give free listeners a reason to subscribe for the rest.
- **Explain what the paid tier includes.** Mention it at the start or end of episodes and in episode descriptions. Describe free and paid benefits on your About page.
- **Publish paid episodes on a regular schedule.** Subscribers should know what they get each week or month.
- **Give paid subscribers a way to participate.** Answer their questions in a mailbag episode or talk with them between episodes. Shea Serrano, for example, invites paid subscribers into the conversation with [Substack Chat](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships). You can also organize a paid-subscriber community into channels.

Substack is also adding [podcast sponsorships](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships), allowing earnings from ads as well as subscriptions. Dynamic sponsorships, described as being in early access, let creators run campaigns with their own sponsors and update ads across their back catalog without re-editing episodes.

For other revenue options, see [how to make money podcasting](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/make-money).

### Frequently asked questions

#### Is it free to start a paid podcast?

Yes, on Substack. Hosting is free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees, and you pay nothing until you earn. With paid subscriptions, you keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees. See [how to start a podcast for free](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/for-free) for the rest of a free setup.

#### How much should I charge for a paid podcast?

For Substack accounts paid in US dollars, the minimum is $5 a month and $30 a year. Serious Trouble charges $6 a month or $60 a year. You can add a founding member plan for listeners who want to pay more and change prices later.

#### Can you put a paid podcast on Spotify and Apple Podcasts?

Yes. Each paid Substack subscriber gets a private RSS feed containing paid episodes, which they can add to Apple Podcasts and other podcast apps. Paid episodes also go to Spotify, where subscribers unlock them by linking their Substack account.

#### Can a podcast have free and paid episodes?

Yes. On Substack, free and paid episodes belong to the same show. You choose the audience for each episode and can add a free preview to a paid episode.

## Podcast ideas and topics for your first show

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-ideas

Explore ideas by interest, audience, and format, then choose a topic you can turn into a series of episodes.

Last updated: October 22, 2026 · By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack

### What makes a good podcast topic?

A good podcast topic has four things:

- A specific audience.
- A reason for that audience to come back every week.
- A host with knowledge of or access to the subject.
- Enough material for at least 50 episodes.

A specific audience matters most. Podcasts that last are rarely about an overly broad topic; they typically focus on a niche subject for people who care a lot about it.

For example, [Drop Your Buffs](https://dropyourbuffs.substack.com/), from Sean Ross and Evan Ross Katz, [started as a show about *Survivor* and now covers other TV shows too](https://on.substack.com/p/culture-captured-in-real-time). It has a 4.5-star average from more than 1,200 ratings.

This guide is part of Substack's [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### Podcast ideas by interest and audience

Good podcast ideas usually start with something you already care about and a group of people who care about it too. These ideas span 11 interests, each paired with a show on Substack that has found an audience. Use the shows for inspiration, not as templates, and bring your own angle, voice, and experience.

#### TV and film podcast ideas

- **Recaps of the shows you watch.** For fans who want to talk after each episode. [Drop Your Buffs](https://dropyourbuffs.substack.com/), from Sean Ross and Evan Ross Katz, recaps *Survivor* and other TV shows and interviews former contestants.
- **Ranking your favorites.** For fans who like an argument. [Organizing Things](https://goodmovie.substack.com/), from Shea Serrano and Jason Concepcion, sorts one movie subject per episode into Great, Good, Meh, or Bad.
- **The business of movies.** For fans who follow what sells. Scott Mendelson's [The Box Office Podcast](https://scottmendelson.substack.com/) is a weekly conversation about the weekend box office.

#### Sports podcast ideas

- **One sport, covered closely.** For fans who want more than national highlights. [Split Zone Duo](https://www.splitzoneduo.com/) covers college football.
- **One team.** For fans who follow every game. [The Bill and Doug Show](https://www.billanddougshow.com/) covers Ohio State football, and [Browns Film Breakdown](https://www.brownsfilmbreakdown.com/) analyzes the Cleveland Browns.
- **A sport you do, not only watch.** For skiers, runners, and anyone who plays. [The Storm Skiing Journal and Podcast](https://www.stormskiing.com/), from Stuart Winchester, covers ski resorts and the people who run them, with interviews and industry news.

#### Food podcast ideas

- **Conversations with people in food.** For readers who follow bakers, chefs, and cookbook authors. [David Lebovitz](https://davidlebovitz.substack.com/) talks with bakers, pastry chefs, chocolatiers, and cookbook authors from his kitchen in Paris.
- **Weeknight cooking.** For home cooks who need dinner ideas. Caroline Chambers's [What To Cook When You Don't Feel Like Cooking](https://whattocook.substack.com/) includes The What To Cook Show, which talks through simple weeknight recipes.
- **Food and health.** For people who cook with their health in mind. [Brain Health Kitchen](https://brainhealthkitchen.substack.com/), from physician Annie Fenn, talks with doctors and researchers about food, habits, and brain health.
- **Food culture.** For listeners interested in the people and business behind cooking and dining. [Vittles](https://www.vittlesmagazine.com/), a food and culture magazine from the UK and India, interviews chefs, bakers, and writers about the food business.

#### Books and writing podcast ideas

- **A slow read of one book.** For readers who want company through a long book. [Close Reads](https://closereads.substack.com/) reads one book a few chapters at a time.
- **The great books, studied together.** For readers who want to work through the classics. [Athenaeum Book Club](https://athenaeumbooks.com/) is a digital book club that studies the great texts of Western civilization, from *The Odyssey* to *The Brothers Karamazov*.

#### History podcast ideas

- **The history behind the news.** For listeners who want context for current events. [Letters from an American](https://heathercoxrichardson.substack.com/podcast), from historian Heather Cox Richardson, connects today's political news to American history.
- **One story per episode.** For listeners who like a story with a beginning and an end. [The Humanity Archive](https://thehumanityarchive.substack.com/), from Jermaine Fowler, tells lesser-known stories from history.

#### Science, technology, and ideas podcast ideas

- **Long-form interviews with experts.** For curious listeners who want depth, not headlines. [Dwarkesh Podcast](https://www.dwarkesh.com/) publishes long interviews with researchers, historians, and technology leaders.
- **Explaining new research.** For non-specialists who see science in the news. [Inside Medicine](https://insidemedicine.substack.com/), from emergency physician Jeremy Faust, explains new medical research and public health news.
- **One field in depth.** For listeners who want to understand one subject well. [Volts](https://www.volts.wtf/), from David Roberts, covers clean energy and climate policy.

#### Politics and news podcast ideas

- **Analysis for a specific audience.** For listeners who want context, not a stream of headlines. [Pantsuit Politics](https://www.pantsuitpoliticsshow.com/), from Sarah Stewart Holland and Beth Silvers, talks through the latest political news.
- **Elections and voters.** For listeners who follow campaigns and polls. [GD Politics](https://www.gdpolitics.com/), from Galen Druke, covers elections, polling, and what voters think.
- **The law, explained.** For listeners who want to understand court cases and legal news. [Serious Trouble](https://www.serioustrouble.show/), from Josh Barro and Ken White, talks through the legal stories in the news.

#### Business and work podcast ideas

- **One industry, from the inside.** For people in that industry or trying to enter it. [The Pragmatic Engineer](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/), from Gergely Orosz, interviews engineers and engineering leaders about how software is built at large tech companies and startups.
- **Career and product advice.** For people who build products. [Lenny's Podcast](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/), from Lenny Rachitsky, interviews product leaders and founders about building products and growing a career.
- **Business news, explained.** For listeners who want analysis, not headlines. [Prof G Media](https://www.profgmedia.com/), from Scott Galloway, analyzes the forces changing business, technology, and the economy.

#### Personal life, health, and family podcast ideas

- **Relationships.** For listeners who want to understand their relationships. Psychotherapist Esther Perel's [Entre Nous](https://estherperel.substack.com/) explores love, desire, and relationships.
- **Health in midlife.** For people over 40 who want to stay active. [Notes on Midlife Fitness](https://howardluksmd.substack.com/), from orthopedic surgeon Howard Luks, explains how to stay strong and active as you age.
- **A language you are learning.** For learners who want to hear the language as people speak it. [French With Frederic](https://www.frenchwithfrederic.com/) teaches modern Quebec French through Quebec culture.

#### Hobby podcast ideas

- **A listening club.** For music fans who want to hear albums with others. Steven Hyden's [Catalog Club](https://stevenhyden.substack.com/) is “like a book club, but for albums.”
- **Gardening.** For people who spend their weekends in the garden. [Grow Like Wild!](https://rebeccamcmackin.substack.com/), from horticulturist Rebecca McMackin, covers ecological gardening.
- **Video games.** For people who play a lot of games. [CORE](https://www.core.show/) is a weekly video game show.

#### Literature and storytelling podcast ideas

- **Classic stories, read aloud.** For listeners who want to hear great literature. Ruby Love's [Classics Read Aloud](https://classicsreadaloud.substack.com/) reads classic short stories, fairy tales, and excerpts from novels.
- **Stories read by their author.** For listeners who like audiobooks and short fiction. In [Alphabet Soup](https://etgarkeret.substack.com/), Etgar Keret reads his own short stories.

### How to validate your podcast idea before launch

Check what already exists, talk to five people in your intended audience, and record a short pilot that a few of them hear before you launch.

1. **Review existing shows.** Browse the Apple Podcasts and Spotify charts in your category, and search both apps for your topic. Listen to two or three episodes of the closest shows and write down what they do not cover.
2. **Talk to five people in your audience.** Ask what they listen to now, what they wish existed, and when they would listen: on a commute, during a workout, or while cooking.
3. **Ask your existing readers or followers.** If you write a newsletter, ask subscribers which topic they would listen to. On Substack, you can post the question in Notes or your subscriber Chat.
4. **Record a 10-minute pilot.** Send it to the same five people, or publish it as a trailer.

Ask pilot listeners:

- In one sentence, what is this show about?
- Who would you send it to?
- Where did you stop listening, and why?
- Would you listen to the next episode?

**Signs the premise needs work:** listeners describe the show in different ways, nobody can name a person to send it to, or most people stop in the first two minutes.

For recording guidance, see [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording).

### Turn your topic into your first five episodes

A show topic is what the podcast is about every week. An episode topic is one question inside it that a listener could search for. Plan your first five episodes before launch so you know the show has range.

- **Phrase each episode as a question a listener would ask.** The same words make a good episode title and a good search term.
- **Mix formats.** One interview in the first five episodes shows listeners the range of the show.
- **Dedicate an episode to listener questions.** This shows new listeners that the show responds to its audience and gives you topics for the next season.

To turn each plan into an outline, see [podcast script templates](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-script).

### What if your podcast topic feels too broad or too crowded?

If your topic feels too broad, add a specific audience, place, time period, or format. If it feels too crowded, look at how many shows are still publishing: far fewer than directory counts suggest.

A specific premise makes the show easy to describe in one sentence, which is how listeners recommend podcasts to each other.

According to [CastFox Research (2026)](https://www.castfox.net/research/podcast-statistics-2026):

- About 4.8 million podcast feeds exist.
- Only about 530,000 shows, or 11%, published an episode in 2026.
- Of all podcasts, 23% have only one episode, and 53% have six episodes or fewer.

A show that keeps publishing past episode six already has more episodes than over half of all podcasts.

#### Next step: from premise to show identity

Once you can describe your show in one sentence, you have what you need to name it. See [podcast name ideas](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-names).

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is the best topic for a first podcast?

The best topic is one you know well, for an audience you can describe in one sentence, with enough material for at least 50 episodes. Specific topics are [easier to grow](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience) than broad ones because listeners can tell immediately who the show is for.

#### How do I find a podcast niche?

List the subjects you already talk about, read about, or get asked about. For each one, name a specific audience and an angle that existing shows do not cover. Then score the ideas on audience need, your interest, access, difference, ease, and cost.

#### Can I start a podcast about my newsletter topic?

Yes. Your readers are your first listeners, and you can turn posts into episodes or read them aloud. On Substack, a podcast lives in the same publication as your newsletter, so each episode goes to your existing subscribers by email.

#### How many episodes should I plan before launch?

Plan at least five episodes and record two or three before launch. A plan shows whether the topic has range, and launching with more than one episode gives new listeners more to hear.

#### Is it too late to start a podcast?

No. About 43% of actively publishing podcasts are less than a year old, according to [CastFox Research (2026)](https://www.castfox.net/research/podcast-statistics-2026). New shows start every week, and most stop after a few episodes, so a show that publishes consistently on a regular schedule has an opportunity to stand out.

### Starting a podcast on Substack

Substack says you can start a podcast for free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees. Episodes go to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and your subscribers' inboxes.

## Podcast name ideas: how to name your show

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-names

### What makes a good podcast name?

A good podcast name is easy to say and remember, tells listeners something about the show, is not already used by another podcast, and still fits if the show changes over time.

Use this checklist for every name you consider:

- **Easy to say:** Someone can recommend it out loud without spelling it.
- **Easy to remember:** A listener can find it again after hearing it once.
- **Relevant:** It hints at the topic, tone, or audience.
- **Distinct:** No other podcast or well-known brand in a related field uses it.
- **Flexible:** It still works if the show adds guests, changes format, or broadens its subject.

Most podcast names are short. An analysis of over 600,000 podcasts found that the median show title was **20 characters**, and **75% were 29 characters or shorter**. About **one in five** included the word “podcast” ([Inside Radio](https://www.insideradio.com/podcastnewsdaily/podcast-name-calling-the-shorter-the-better/article_234866e6-71b3-11e9-a9b2-9351feb9c1cb.html)).

A name alone does not determine whether listeners find your show. Your description, episode titles, and recommendations also matter. Use the name to make the show memorable, rather than to fit in search keywords.

This guide is part of the [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast). If you have not chosen a topic, see [podcast ideas and topics](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-ideas).

### Podcast name ideas by style

Choose a naming pattern first, then the words.

| Style | How it works | Real example on Substack | More examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Describes the format | Tells listeners what happens in each episode | [Organizing Things](https://goodmovie.substack.com/): two hosts sort one movie subject per episode into tiers | *The Slow Read*; *One Dish*; *Ask the Ref* |
| An insider phrase | Uses words fans of the subject recognize | [Drop Your Buffs](https://dropyourbuffs.substack.com/): a phrase from *Survivor*, for a *Survivor* podcast | *Low and Slow* (barbecue); *Second Draft* (writing); *Full Count* (baseball) |
| Wordplay | Uses puns or twists on familiar phrases | [Split Zone Duo](https://www.splitzoneduo.com/): a play on football terminology, for a college football show | *Knead to Know* (baking); *Plot Twist* (books) |
| The host’s name | Builds on an audience that already knows the host | [Dwarkesh Podcast](https://www.dwarkesh.com/): the host’s first name, for an interview show | *[Your name] Explains*; *Talks with [Your name]* |
| Alliteration or rhythm | Uses repeated sounds to aid recall | [Pantsuit Politics](https://www.pantsuitpoliticsshow.com/): repeated P sounds, for a political show | *Budget Bites*; *Garden Gossip* |
| Short and evocative | Uses two or three words that suggest a mood or subject | [Volts](https://www.volts.wtf/): one short word suggesting energy, for a clean energy show | *Night Shift*; *Open Kitchen* |

#### Which style should you choose?

- **Starting with no audience:** A name describing the format or topic helps new listeners understand the show from its title alone.
- **Already known for your writing or work:** Your own name, alone or in the title, tells your existing audience it is you.
- **For a devoted community:** An insider phrase signals that the show is made by and for fans.

### How to come up with a podcast name

Start with five questions. Your answers provide the words, subject, and tone to build names from:

1. Who is the listener?
2. What does the show promise them?
3. What is the subject, in three words?
4. What is the tone?
5. What words does this audience use?

Write down as many ideas as you can using your answers and the six naming styles. Do not judge them yet. Once you have a list, check which names are taken, then test your favorites out loud and at thumbnail size.

### How to check whether a podcast name is already taken

Search podcast apps, the web, social media, and trademark databases. These searches help identify whether listeners could confuse your show with another one; **they are not legal clearance**.

#### Discoverability checklist

- **Apple Podcasts and Spotify:** Search for the same name and close variations.
- **YouTube:** Search there too, because many podcasts are published as video.
- **Podcast search engines:** Tools such as Listen Notes and Podcast Index search many podcast directories at once.
- **Substack:** Search in the Substack app and on substack.com.
- **The web:** Search the name in quotation marks and review the first two pages of results.
- **Social media:** Check handle availability on the platforms where you will promote the show.
- **A web address:** Check whether your Substack address (`yourname.substack.com`) or a custom domain is available.

#### Trademark check

In the US, copyright does not cover names and short titles, so a podcast name is protected by trademark instead. Before committing, search the trademark database for each country where you expect listeners:

- **United States:** [USPTO trademark search](https://tmsearch.uspto.gov/).
- **Canada:** [Canadian Trademarks Database](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/cipo/trademark-search).
- **European Union:** [EUIPO trademark search](https://euipo.europa.eu/eSearch/).

Look for names that sound alike or have similar spellings, not just exact matches. In the US, the trademark office considers podcasts and radio programs closely related, so an earlier radio show with a similar name can block a podcast’s trademark application ([Mondaq, June 2026](https://www.mondaq.com/unitedstates/trademark/1801446/podcast-trademarks-protecting-your-brand-in-a-booming-medium)).

This is general information, not legal advice. If you plan to invest heavily in a name, or your searches find something close, ask a trademark lawyer for a full search.

### Test your podcast name out loud and at thumbnail size

Test each finalist with someone who has not seen it written, and on a small square cover the size of a phone-screen thumbnail.

#### The out-loud test

1. **Say the name to a friend once without spelling it.** Ask them to type it into a podcast app. If they type it incorrectly, listeners recommending your show by word of mouth may too.
2. **Ask them the next day what the show was called.** A name they remember after one hearing passes.
3. **Say it in a sentence:** “Welcome to *[name]*, the show about …” If it sounds awkward, you will notice it in every episode intro.

Watch for unusual spellings, numbers that could be written as words (“4” or “four”), and words that sound like other words.

#### The thumbnail test

Listeners often first see your show as a small square in a podcast app, search results, or recommendations. Put each name on a simple mock cover and shrink it to about the size of a phone app icon.

- **Short names** can use large type and remain readable as thumbnails.
- **Long names** become small text. Consider a shorter main title with the rest as a tagline in the show description.

See [podcast cover art examples](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cover-art) for more on designing covers that work at small sizes.

### Write your show’s one-sentence promise

Pair your name with a sentence explaining who the show is for and what they get from it. The name makes the show memorable; the promise tells a new listener why to press play.

Use this pattern:

**[Show name] is a [format] for [listener] about [subject], so they can [benefit].**

For example, Substack’s [Open Tab](https://on.substack.com/s/open-tab) is an interview show for writers and creators about how independent media founders built their businesses, so they can learn what it takes to build their own.

### Finalize your podcast name and move toward launch

Use the same spelling and capitalization everywhere:

- Put the name on your [podcast cover art](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cover-art).
- Enter the name, description, and category in your podcast host. These details travel to Apple Podcasts and Spotify through your RSS feed. See [podcast RSS feed and show details](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).
- Claim social media handles and a web address that use the name.
- Say the name in your spoken intro.

**On Substack**, your podcast can share your publication’s name or have a separate name. You enter it once during setup, and Substack uses it in your RSS feed, the Substack app, and your podcast page.

#### Can you change a podcast name later?

Yes. Change the name in your podcast host, and podcast apps update through your RSS feed. Existing followers keep receiving episodes. A change after you have an audience can confuse new listeners, so it is worth choosing carefully before launch.

To change the name on Substack:

1. Open your publication’s **Settings**.
2. Scroll to **Podcasts** and select **Edit** next to your podcast.
3. Change the podcast title under **Basics**.
4. Select **Save podcast settings**.

The new name appears in your RSS feed immediately. Spotify and Apple Podcasts can take **up to 24 hours** to show it.

For the remaining launch steps, see the [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### Frequently asked questions

#### How do I come up with a podcast name?

Answer the five questions about your listener, promise, subject in three words, tone, and audience vocabulary. Brainstorm names in different styles, then check that your favorites are easy to say, remember, and find.

#### Should my podcast name include my own name?

Include it if people already know you from your writing, work, or social media. If you are starting without an audience, a name describing the topic or format usually tells new listeners more.

#### Should I put the word “podcast” in my podcast name?

It is not necessary. About one in five titles includes it, according to the [Pacific Content research cited by Inside Radio](https://www.insideradio.com/podcastnewsdaily/podcast-name-calling-the-shorter-the-better/article_234866e6-71b3-11e9-a9b2-9351feb9c1cb.html). Podcast apps already show listeners that it is a podcast.

#### How long should a podcast name be?

Short enough to read on a small cover. The median title is 20 characters, and 75% are 29 characters or shorter, according to the same research.

#### Can two podcasts have the same name?

It happens, but it makes your show harder to find and can lead to a trademark dispute. Search podcast apps and trademark databases before choosing a name.

#### Can I change my podcast name later?

Yes. Change it in your podcast host; podcast apps update through your RSS feed, and existing followers keep receiving episodes.

## Podcast script templates and examples

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-script

### Podcast scripts: choosing a format

Start with a template for a solo, interview, or co-host episode, then turn it into an outline you can record from.

Last updated: October 22, 2026 · By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack

### What is a podcast script, and do you need one?

A podcast script is a written plan for an episode: what you say to open, the points or questions you cover, and how you close. Many podcasters do not read a script word for word. Instead, they write out the opening and closing and keep the rest as short notes, so the episode stays organized while sounding conversational.

A full script makes sense when the exact words matter, such as an essay or a story read aloud. For example, historian Heather Cox Richardson’s [Letters from an American](https://heathercoxrichardson.substack.com/podcast) publishes an audio version of each written letter, so the letter itself is the script.

This guide is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### What is the basic structure of a podcast episode?

Most episodes have five parts, in this order:

1. **Hook:** The first few seconds give listeners a reason to keep listening. This can be a line from you or a short clip of the most interesting moment from your guest.
2. **Introduction:** The show name, your name, and, for an interview, who the guest is.
3. **Main segment:** The points or questions you plan to cover, in order.
4. **Summary:** A short recap of the most important point or best answer.
5. **Closing:** A thank-you, what comes next, and how to subscribe.

The typical podcast episode runs 35 minutes, and half of all shows have episodes between 18 and 56 minutes long ([CastFox Research](https://www.castfox.net/research/podcast-statistics-2026), 2026). Keep the hook and introduction short so listeners reach the main segment within the first minute or two.

### Solo podcast script template

Use this template for an episode you host alone. Write the hook, introduction, and closing word for word. Keep the main segment as short notes so you sound like you are talking, not reading.

**Solo episode script**

- **Show:** [Show name]
- **Episode:** [Number and title]
- **Target length:** [Minutes]

**Hook — word for word**

> “[One sentence about the question, problem, or story this episode covers.]”

**Introduction — word for word**

> “Welcome to [show name]. I'm [your name], and this is the show about [your topic, in a few words]. Today: [this episode's topic].”

**Main segment — notes only**

- Point 1: [Point] — [a story, example, or fact that supports it]
- Point 2: [Point] — [a story, example, or fact that supports it]
- Point 3: [Point] — [a story, example, or fact that supports it]

**Summary — notes only**

[The one idea you want listeners to remember]

**Closing — word for word**

> “Thanks for listening to [show name]. Next time: [next episode's topic]. To get every episode by email, subscribe on Substack at [your publication's address].”

When an episode is a story or essay read aloud, the written text becomes the whole script. Examples on Substack include:

- [Alphabet Soup](https://etgarkeret.substack.com/), where writer Etgar Keret reads his own short stories.
- [Classics Read Aloud](https://classicsreadaloud.substack.com/), where Ruby Love reads classic short stories, fairy tales, and excerpts from novels.

### Interview podcast script template

For an interview, write your introduction, your guest’s introduction, and your questions. **Do not script the answers.** Your notes keep the conversation on track, and your guest’s answers keep it natural.

**Interview episode script**

- **Guest:** [Name and what they do]
- **Topic:** [A few words]
- **Target length:** [Minutes]

**Hook — word for word**

> “[The most interesting thing your guest has done or said, in one sentence.]”

**Introduction — word for word**

> “Welcome to [show name]. I'm [your name]. My guest today is [guest's name], [one line about who they are]. [Guest's first name], thanks for joining me.”

**Questions**

1. [A question about how the guest got started]
2. [A question about the main topic]
3. [A follow-up, such as “What happened next?” or “Why?”]
4. [A question about a specific story or example]
5. [A question about what listeners can do with this]
6. [A last question, such as “What are you working on next?”]

**Closing — word for word**

> “[Guest's name], thank you. Where can people find your work?”

[Guest answers]

> “Thanks for listening to [show name]. To get every episode by email, subscribe on Substack at [your publication's address].”

**Interview preparation and follow-ups**

- Send your guest the topic and a few questions before you record.
- Write open questions that start with *how*, *why*, or *what*, so answers are longer than yes or no.
- Listen to each answer and follow up on it, even if that means skipping a question on your list.

The template supplies the questions; your follow-ups turn them into a conversation. Examples include:

- [Dwarkesh Podcast](https://www.dwarkesh.com/), hosted by Dwarkesh Patel, publishes long interviews with researchers, historians, and technology leaders. Most of its recent episodes run more than an hour.
- Substack’s [Open Tab](https://on.substack.com/s/open-tab) hosts conversations with media founders.

If you record in the [Substack Recording Studio](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording), your guest joins by invitation. On a computer, you can share your screen to show a chart, article, or anything else your questions refer to.

### Co-host podcast script template

Co-hosts usually work from a shared outline instead of a script: who opens, which topics come in which order, and who leads each one. Share the outline with your co-host before recording.

**Co-host episode outline**

- **Hosts:** [Host A], [Host B]
- **Episode:** [Number and title]
- **Target length:** [Minutes]

**Opening — [Host A]**

> “Welcome to [show name]. I'm [Host A]...”
>
> “...and I'm [Host B]. Today we're talking about [this episode's topic].”

**Topic 1: [Topic] — led by [Host A]**

- [Point or question to discuss]
- [Point or question to discuss]

**Topic 2: [Topic] — led by [Host B]**

- [Point or question to discuss]
- [Point or question to discuss]

**Topic 3: [A listener question or a regular segment] — led by [Host A]**

- [The question, or what the segment covers]

**Closing — [Host B]**

> “That's our show. To get every episode by email, subscribe on Substack at [your publication's address]. See you next [day of the week].”

The outline decides who leads each topic, and the conversation between the hosts does the rest. Examples on Substack include:

- [Pantsuit Politics](https://www.pantsuitpoliticsshow.com/), from Sarah Stewart Holland and Beth Silvers, which talks through the latest political news.
- [Serious Trouble](https://www.serioustrouble.show/), from Josh Barro and Ken White, which talks through legal stories in the news.

### How to write a podcast intro and outro that sound natural and memorable

Your intro and outro are the parts listeners hear in every episode, so they are worth writing word for word.

- **Write the way you talk.** Read the lines aloud and cut any word you stumble over.
- **Keep the intro short:** the show name, your name, and the episode topic, then start.
- **Tell listeners what they get from the episode**, rather than listing everything you will cover.
- **Ask for one thing in the outro:** subscribe, share the episode, or leave a comment.
- **Use the same wording in every episode** so listeners recognize your show from the first line.

**Intro lines you can copy**

> “This is [show name], the show about [your topic]. I'm [your name].”

> “On [show name] this week: [the episode's topic, in one sentence].”

**Outro lines you can copy**

> “If you liked this episode, subscribe on Substack at [your publication's address] to get the next one in your inbox.”

> “Have a question for a future episode? Leave a comment on this episode on Substack.”

On Substack, each episode is also a post, so listeners can comment on it. You can send each new episode to subscribers by email and in the Substack app.

### How to turn a podcast script into an outline you can record from

1. **Read your script aloud once and time it.** If it runs long, cut a point instead of talking faster.
2. **Reduce everything except the hook, introduction, and closing** to a few words per point.
3. **Put the outline where you can see it while recording**, on paper or a second screen.
4. **Mark where you will stop** for a guest or co-host to speak.
5. **After recording, turn the outline into show notes.** On Substack, the show notes you add to an episode become its description in Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

You do not need to publish your script for listeners who want to read along. Substack automatically creates a transcript of every podcast episode, and you can edit it or name the speakers before publishing.

For recording guidance, see [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording).

### Frequently asked questions

#### Do podcasters use scripts?

Many podcasters use an outline instead of a full script. They write the opening and closing word for word and keep the rest as notes, so the episode stays organized and sounds natural. Shows that read an essay or story aloud, such as audio versions of newsletter posts, use a full script.

#### How long is a podcast script for a 30-minute episode?

A word-for-word script for a 30-minute episode is about **4,500 words**, based on an average US conversation rate of around **150 words a minute**. Your pace may be faster or slower, so read your script aloud and time it.

#### Should I write a script for an interview podcast?

Write your introduction, your guest’s introduction, and a list of questions, but not your guest’s answers. A full script makes an interview sound rehearsed. Send your guest the topic and a few questions before recording so they can prepare.

### Publishing a podcast on Substack

The page states that you can start a podcast for free on Substack, record in the Substack Recording Studio or upload audio, and publish to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and subscribers’ inboxes, with no hosting fees and no platform fees.

## How to record a podcast: a beginner's guide

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording

Record your first episode with the equipment you already have, from setting up your room to recording remote guests.

Last updated: October 22, 2026 · By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack

### How do you record a podcast?

You can record a podcast for free with a phone or computer in five steps:

1. Choose your recording setup.
2. Prepare your episode.
3. Set up your room and microphone.
4. Make a test recording.
5. Record your episode.

This guide is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### Choose your recording setup

The best way to record depends on how many people are on the show and where they are. A solo host can record almost anywhere, while remote guests need a tool that connects everyone over the internet. The free Substack Recording Studio lets you invite up to two guests by their Substack handles and records the whole conversation.

| Setup | Best for | What you need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Substack Recording Studio | Solo episodes and interviews with up to two remote guests, on video or audio only | A Substack publication with at least 10 free subscribers, and a computer with a web browser or a phone with the Substack app |
| A live stream on Substack, published afterward as an episode | Shows that want listeners to join while they record | A Substack publication, and a computer with a web browser or a phone with the Substack app |
| Recording straight into a Substack audio post | Short solo episodes | A Substack account and a microphone |
| A voice recorder app | Solo episodes recorded anywhere | A phone or computer |
| A remote-recording tool, such as Riverside or Descript | Interviews where each person’s audio is recorded on their own device | An account with the tool; free plans have limits |

You can go live on Substack with video or in audio-only mode, then publish the recording as an episode when the stream ends. Live streams work well for Q&A episodes because listeners can comment and ask questions in real time.

If you [record video on Substack](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast), the episode’s audio goes to podcast apps automatically.

### Prepare your episode

Write a short outline with an opening that explains the episode, the main points you want to cover, and a closing that tells listeners how to subscribe. You do not need a full script.

- **Prepare guests:** Send the topic and a few questions in advance, and agree on how long you will record. For the Substack Recording Studio, ask for their Substack handles so you can invite them.
- **Reduce distractions:** Turn off notifications on your phone and computer, and close unnecessary apps.
- **Keep water nearby:** A dry mouth makes sounds the microphone picks up. A sip during a pause helps keep your voice clear.

For outlines you can copy, see [podcast script templates](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-script).

### Set up your room and microphone

Record in the smallest, quietest room available, and keep the microphone about one hand-width from your mouth. Soft surfaces absorb sound and reduce echo, so a small, furnished room usually sounds better than a large, empty one.

- Turn off fans, air conditioning, and appliances that hum.
- Keep the microphone at the same distance throughout the episode; moving closer or farther changes your volume.
- Speak across the microphone rather than straight into it to soften bursts of air on sounds like “p” and “b.”
- Wear headphones, and ask remote guests to do the same so their speakers do not echo into their microphones.

A phone’s built-in microphone or wired earbuds with a microphone are enough to start. The Substack app supports recording on your phone in the Recording Studio. A USB microphone is the upgrade that makes the most impact on sound quality. See [podcast equipment for beginners](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/equipment) for what to buy first.

### Make a test recording

Before every session, record about **30 seconds** of yourself speaking at your normal volume, then listen on headphones. Your voice should sound clear and steady, without crackling when you laugh or speak loudly.

- If your recording tool has a level meter, keep your loudest moments well below the top. If it reaches the top or turns red, move back from the microphone or lower its input volume.
- If your voice sounds faint or distant, move closer before raising the volume.
- If you hear echo, add soft surfaces or move to a smaller room.
- With a guest, listen to a short test of their audio too. Problems are easier to fix before the conversation starts.

### Record your episode

Start recording, then wait a few seconds before speaking so your first words are not cut off. If you make a small slip, keep going: listeners expect a natural conversation, not a perfect one.

#### How to set up the Substack Recording Studio

Any publication with **at least 10 free subscribers** can use the Recording Studio. It is free and works on the web and in the Substack app for iPhone and Android.

1. On the web, select **Create**, then **Recording studio**.
2. Allow Substack to use your microphone and camera when your browser asks.
3. Use the **Mic** and **Video** controls at the bottom of the screen to check your microphone and camera. You can record with your camera on or use audio only.
4. To invite guests, enter each guest’s Substack handle. A recording can have **up to three people: you and two guests**. Guests receive a pop-up, push notification, or email invitation and join from a computer with a web browser or a phone with the Substack app.

Before starting, you can add your publication’s logo or wordmark to the video under **Brand and effects** and choose where it appears on screen.

#### How to record in the Substack Recording Studio

1. Select **Start recording**. Substack takes about **20 seconds** to connect, then a red **Recording** label appears at the top of the screen.
2. To show slides, a website, or an app, select **Share screen**. Screen sharing works best in Google Chrome.
3. Select **End** to stop recording.
4. Substack creates a post with your recording. Save it to drafts or publish it immediately. Substack emails you a link when the draft is ready.

After recording, Substack makes short clips you can share and a thumbnail you can change. Screen sharing works well for demos: Azeem Azhar of Exponential View used it to [show viewers how he runs his AI agent system](https://www.exponentialview.co/p/behind-the-scenes-of-my-ai-agent).

When your episode is published, see [how to get your podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can I record a podcast on my phone?

Yes. Use your phone’s voice recorder app or the Substack app, where you can use the Recording Studio or go live. A phone’s built-in microphone is enough to start. Record in a small, quiet room and hold the phone at the same distance throughout.

#### How do I record a podcast remotely with a guest?

Use a tool that connects you over the internet and records the conversation, such as the Substack Recording Studio. Invite up to two guests by their Substack handles; they can join from a computer with a web browser or a phone with the Substack app. Ask guests to wear headphones and record from a quiet room.

#### Should I record audio and video at the same time?

On Substack, you do not need to record them separately. When you publish a video episode, its audio goes to podcast apps automatically. If you prefer not to be on camera, you can record audio only.

#### Is there free podcast recording software?

Yes. The Substack Recording Studio is free and built into Substack. You can record solo or with up to two remote guests, on video or audio only, and publish the recording as an episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other podcast apps.

For solo episodes, your phone’s voice recorder app also works. Remote-recording tools such as Riverside and Descript offer free plans with limits.

#### What audio format should I record a podcast in?

Record in the highest quality your tool allows. To upload an episode to Substack, use an **MP3, WAV, or AAC** file.

### Publishing and fees on Substack

Recordings can be published to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and subscribers’ inboxes, with no hosting fees and no platform fees.

## What is a podcast RSS feed? How to create and use one

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed

### What is a podcast RSS feed?

A podcast RSS feed is a web address that lists your show's details and all its episodes. Podcast apps check it to find and download new episodes. RSS stands for **Really Simple Syndication**. You submit the feed to each app once; after that, newly published episodes appear in those apps automatically.

Your podcast host creates and updates the feed, so you do not need to write or edit it yourself. On Substack, the feed is created for free when you set up a podcast.

Using a feed involves three steps:

1. Create your podcast RSS feed.
2. Publish an episode to your feed.
3. Submit your feed to listening apps.

This guide is part of Substack's [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### What information does a podcast RSS feed contain?

A feed contains information about the show, which apps display on your show page, and information about each episode, including a link to its audio file.

**Show details:**

- Title
- Description
- Cover art
- Author or byline
- Language
- Categories
- Whether the show has explicit content

**Episode details:**

- Title
- Description or show notes
- A link to the audio file
- Publication date
- Length
- Whether the episode has explicit content
- Episode art, if added

On Substack, show details come from the **Basics** section of your podcast settings. Changes made there appear in your feed immediately.

For cover-art dimensions and file types, see [podcast cover art examples, sizes, and templates](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cover-art).

### How to create a podcast RSS feed on Substack

Substack automatically creates your podcast RSS feed at no cost when you set up a podcast. To find its web address:

1. Open your publication's **Settings** and scroll to **Podcasts**.
2. Select **Edit** next to your podcast.
3. Scroll to **Distribution** and copy your RSS feed URL.

Podcast apps accept your feed only after you publish at least one episode. If you are not ready for a full episode, publish a short trailer introducing the show.

If you have not set up a podcast, see [how to start a podcast for free](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/for-free).

### How to publish an episode to your feed

Publishing an episode on your podcast host automatically adds it to your RSS feed. Podcast apps pick it up the next time they check the feed. Apps check on their own schedules, so an episode can take **up to 24 hours** to appear and may appear in one app before another.

On Substack, each published episode goes to your feed, the Substack app, and your subscribers' email inboxes. To add artwork for an individual episode, open its Publish page, then **Episode metadata**, and upload an image under **Episode art**.

Substack counts downloads using the IAB Tech Lab's industry standard: a download counts when at least **60 seconds** of an episode is downloaded to a unique device within **24 hours**. Download figures are available in your Podcasts dashboard.

For episode production guidance, see [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording) and [how to edit a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/editing).

### How to submit your feed to listening apps

Copy your RSS feed URL from your podcast host and submit it through each app's tool for podcasters. This is a one-time step for each app. Most podcast apps take their listings from Apple Podcasts, so [submitting to Apple](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts) reaches many of them at once.

For example, [Open Tab](https://on.substack.com/s/open-tab), Substack's interview show with media founders, is published on Substack and reaches listeners on [Apple Podcasts](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/open-tab/id1896276138) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/0GuEw5OM6FwgzRXNfnhmD7).

#### Apple Podcasts

1. In your Substack podcast settings, scroll to the Apple Podcasts section and select **Copy URL**.
2. Select **Visit Apple Podcasts Connect** and sign in with your Apple ID. In Apple Podcasts Connect, select **Add (+)**, then **New Show**.
3. Choose **Add a show with an RSS feed**, paste your feed URL, and select **Add**. Check your show's details, select **Save**, and publish your show.
4. Once the show is published, copy its Apple Podcasts link into your Substack podcast settings so a “Listen on Apple” link appears on your episodes.

#### Spotify

On Substack, you do not need to submit an RSS feed to Spotify. In your podcast settings, go to **Distribution → Spotify → Connect to Spotify** and confirm.

Your show appears on Spotify within about **an hour**, and new episodes sync automatically after publication. Publish at least one free or paid episode before connecting.

#### Other apps

Substack's podcast settings list other apps you can submit to, with a direct link to each. After submitting, paste each app's link to your show back into your settings so it appears on your episode pages.

### What is a private podcast RSS feed?

A private podcast RSS feed is an address unique to one listener, used to deliver episodes that only subscribers can hear. A public feed is the feed submitted to podcast apps, which anyone can follow.

On Substack, every subscriber receives a unique private RSS feed. A paid subscriber's feed includes both paid and free episodes, allowing them to listen in the podcast app they already use. Subscribers can add their private feed from their **Manage subscription** page or the **Listen on** links on any episode.

For a paid episode, you can add a shorter free audio version so listeners without a paid subscription can hear a preview.

Paid episodes can also go to Spotify. Selecting **Connect to Spotify** syncs both free and paid episodes. Paid episodes appear with a lock: paid subscribers unlock them by linking their Substack account, while other listeners can upgrade to a paid subscription from Spotify.

Substack is free to use for free or paid podcasts. If you enable paid subscriptions, you keep **90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees**.

### Why isn't an episode or artwork updating?

An episode or artwork that has not updated is usually waiting for the app to check the feed again. New episodes and changes to show details can take **up to 24 hours** to appear on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

If something is still missing after 24 hours:

- **Apple Podcasts:** Sign in to Apple Podcasts Connect, select your show, and select **Refresh Feed**.
- **YouTube and YouTube Music:** New episodes upload automatically from your feed. You can upload a missed episode yourself in YouTube Studio.
- **Pocket Casts:** Listeners can refresh a show's episode list from its show page.
- **Artwork:** Check that the image meets Apple's requirements: square, at least **1400 × 1400 pixels** and at most **3000 × 3000 pixels**, in **JPEG or PNG** format. Apps often retain the old image for a while after a change.

### What happens when you rename a show or move it to Substack?

Renaming a show or changing its details updates the RSS feed, so existing followers continue receiving episodes.

On Substack, open **Settings → Podcasts**, select **Edit** next to your podcast, and change the title under **Basics**. The new name appears in the feed immediately and in Spotify and Apple Podcasts within **24 hours**. See [podcast name ideas](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/podcast-names) for naming guidance.

To [move a podcast to Substack](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/move-your-podcast) from another host:

1. In your Substack dashboard, select **Podcast → Create podcast → Import an existing podcast**.
2. Paste your current RSS feed URL and select **Submit**. Review the episodes and select **Import all episodes**.
3. Ask your previous host to redirect the old feed to the new Substack feed. This **301 permanent redirect** moves existing followers to the new feed.
4. Submit your new Substack feed to podcast directories.

If you prefer to keep your current host, select **I have a podcast hosted elsewhere → Distribute to Substack** and paste your RSS feed URL. Substack reads your existing feed and publishes new episodes automatically, while your audio, ads, and analytics remain with your current host.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Does Substack give you an RSS feed?

Yes. Substack creates a podcast RSS feed for free when you set up a podcast. Copy its address from your podcast settings to submit it to Apple Podcasts and other apps. Each subscriber also receives a private feed, including paid episodes for paid subscribers.

#### Is a podcast RSS feed free?

Yes. The feed itself costs nothing and comes from your podcast host. Some hosts charge monthly hosting fees, but Substack hosts podcasts with no hosting fees and no platform fees. Paid subscriptions are subject to the revenue share and credit card fees described above. For other hosts' prices, see [how much it costs to start a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/cost).

#### Can I move my podcast to Substack?

Yes. Select **Import an existing podcast** and paste your current RSS feed URL to import your episodes. Then ask your previous host to redirect the old feed to the new Substack feed so podcast apps and followers move with it.

#### Where do I find my podcast RSS feed on Substack?

Open **Settings → Podcasts**, select **Edit** next to your podcast, and scroll to **Distribution** to copy your RSS feed URL.

#### Do I need an RSS feed to get on Spotify?

Not on Substack. Go to **Distribution → Spotify → Connect to Spotify** in your podcast settings. Your show appears within about an hour, without submitting a feed. Publish at least one episode first.

## How to get your podcast on Spotify

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/spotify

### Getting your podcast on Spotify

Connect your show from your podcast host, or submit its RSS feed to Spotify. On Substack, open your podcast settings, select **Spotify**, then **Connect to Spotify**. Your show appears on Spotify within about an hour.

Connecting from Substack is free, with no hosting or platform fees. Free and paid episodes can appear in one Spotify listing, and new episodes sync automatically after publication.

Last updated: October 27, 2026. By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack.

This guide is part of the [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### How podcast submission works

Spotify lists a podcast using its RSS feed—the web address that lists every episode. With most hosts, you copy that address and submit it to Spotify yourself. Some hosts connect directly instead.

Substack connects through Spotify’s Open Access program, allowing Spotify to play both free and paid episodes without a separate feed submission. Learn more about [podcast RSS feeds](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).

### Connect your podcast from Substack

Before connecting:

- Publish at least one free or paid episode. Episodes exclusively for founding members or exclusively for free subscribers do not count.
- Turn off **Private Mode** on Substack; Spotify will not accept your feed while it is on.

To connect:

1. In your publication’s **Settings**, go to **Podcasts** and select **Edit** next to your podcast.
2. Scroll to **Distribute your podcast** and select **Spotify**.
3. Select **Connect to Spotify**.
4. Review the details and select **Connect to Spotify** again.

Your show appears on Spotify within about an hour, and the Spotify card in your settings shows **Connected**. New episodes sync automatically after publication. You cannot choose which episodes sync: every eligible episode goes to Spotify.

Examples include [Open Tab](https://on.substack.com/s/open-tab), Substack’s interview show with independent media founders, which is also [available on Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/0GuEw5OM6FwgzRXNfnhmD7), and [Organizing Things](https://goodmovie.substack.com/podcast), from Shea Serrano and Jason Concepcion. After Shea uploads an episode to Substack, it goes automatically to YouTube, Spotify, and [Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts).

#### Add Spotify links to your Substack pages

Your Substack podcast and episode pages can link to Spotify. Paid subscribers see the paid link; everyone else sees the free link.

1. In your podcast settings, scroll to **Add Spotify links to your Substack pages**.
2. Check **Spotify link for paid subscribers**, which fills in automatically when you connect.
3. Paste your public Spotify show link into **Spotify link for free subscribers**. It can be the same as the paid link.
4. Select **Save**.

#### If your podcast is already on Spotify

When moving an existing Spotify show to Substack, choose between two options:

- **Keep your current Spotify listing:** Select **Manual setup**, then **Copy URL**, and replace your show’s RSS feed with that address in your Spotify for Creators dashboard. You keep your listing and followers, and paid episodes join the same show. Free previews are no longer available on Spotify.
- **Add a separate show for paid episodes:** Select **Connect to Spotify**, then **Do it for me**, and give the paid show a different name. Your free show stays unchanged. This option suits a free feed that relies on free previews or dynamic ads.

**Do not also submit your feed in Spotify for Creators after connecting through Substack.** Doing so creates a duplicate show.

See [how to move your podcast to Substack](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/move-your-podcast) for the full migration steps.

### How paid episodes work on Spotify

Listeners see free and paid episodes in one show:

- **Free episodes** play for everyone.
- **Paid episodes** display a lock. Listeners select **Get access** to link their Substack account.
- **Paid subscribers** who link their account can immediately play paid episodes.
- **Free listeners** who link their account are prompted to upgrade to a monthly, annual, or founding member plan.

Paid subscribers can also link accounts from Substack: on **Manage subscription**, find **Private podcast feeds**, select **Set up podcast**, then **Listen on Spotify**.

Some episode types work differently:

| Episode type | Behavior on Spotify |
|---|---|
| Founding member episodes | Not published to Spotify. |
| Paid episodes with free previews | Free previews are unsupported; the full episode appears locked. |
| Episodes for free subscribers only | Locked to paid subscribers on Spotify. |

See [how to start a paid podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast) for setting up paid episodes and previews.

### Earning money from Spotify listeners

Spotify listeners can upgrade to a paid subscription from Spotify. Paid subscribers who link their accounts unlock your paid episodes there. On Substack, you keep **90% of what you earn, minus credit card fees**.

Substack is also adding [podcast sponsorships](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships):

- **Dynamic sponsorships**, in early access, let you run campaigns with your own sponsors and update ads across your back catalog without re-editing episodes.
- **Third-party sponsorship marketplaces** that fill the ad breaks you mark are coming soon.
- Participation is optional. You decide how many ads run and which kinds of sponsors you accept.

See [how to make money podcasting](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/make-money) for other ways to earn from your show.

### Video episodes on Spotify

When you publish a video episode on Substack, its audio goes to Spotify automatically. To include the video:

1. Open the episode in your Spotify for Creators dashboard.
2. Select **Upload video**.

The uploaded video replaces the audio episode on Spotify and plays only in Spotify’s apps and web player.

See [how to start a video podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast) for recording and publishing guidance.

### Spotify listener numbers

Spotify downloads are included in your Substack podcast download numbers and appear **24 hours after they happen**.

For streams, unique listeners, listening time, and demographics, claim your podcast in Spotify for Creators. Spotify may verify ownership by emailing a code to the address in your RSS feed.

To receive that code:

- Open your publication’s **Settings** and, under **Community**, set **Who can reply to your emails** to **Everyone**.
- You can also change **Email address for RSS feeds** in the **Details** section.

See [how to grow a podcast audience](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience) for ways to reach more listeners.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can you upload a podcast directly to Spotify?

Yes, through Spotify for Creators, which then hosts your show. With Substack, you upload each episode once, and **Connect to Spotify** sends free and paid episodes automatically.

#### Is it free to put a podcast on Spotify?

Yes. Substack hosting and distribution to Spotify are free, with no hosting or platform fees. If you enable paid subscriptions, you keep 90% of earnings, minus credit card fees.

#### How long does it take to appear on Spotify?

About an hour after selecting **Connect to Spotify** on Substack. Subsequent episodes sync automatically when published.

#### Can you put a paid podcast on Spotify?

Yes. Substack sends both free and paid episodes. Paid episodes display a lock, and paid subscribers unlock them by selecting **Get access** and linking their Substack account.

#### Do you need to submit your RSS feed to Spotify?

Not when connecting through Substack. **Connect to Spotify** creates your Spotify show without a separate feed submission. Submitting the feed again through Spotify for Creators creates a duplicate show.

## How to start a video podcast

Source: https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/video-podcast

Record your show on camera with the phone or computer you already have, then publish it as both a video and an audio podcast.

Last updated: October 27, 2026. By [Linda Lebrun](https://substack.com/@linda), Substack.

### How do you start a video podcast?

Choose a format, set up a camera, light, and microphone, then record and publish your episode as video and audio. The guide presents six steps you can complete for free with a phone or computer and the Substack Recording Studio:

1. Choose a video podcast format.
2. Get a camera, a light, and a microphone.
3. Set up your recording space.
4. Record your video podcast.
5. Edit and publish your episode.
6. Share it on YouTube, Spotify, and social media.

This guide is part of Substack’s [complete guide to starting a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast).

### Choose a video podcast format

Your format determines what you need to film. Most video podcasts use one of four setups:

| Format | How it’s filmed | What you need |
|---|---|---|
| Solo show | One host talks to the camera | A phone or webcam, a light, and a microphone |
| Remote interview | Each person records from their own home or office | A tool that records everyone over the internet, such as the Substack Recording Studio |
| In-person conversation | Two or more people at the same table | A camera on each person, or one wide shot, and a microphone for each speaker |
| Live show | You stream to an audience, then publish the recording | A livestream tool, such as live video on Substack |

Video gives your show more places to be found: YouTube, apps, and short clips on social media. According to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/12/substack-launches-a-built-in-recording-studio/), viewers watched more than **700 million hours of podcasts a month on living room devices on YouTube in 2025**, up from about **400 million** the year before. On Substack, creators who had used audio or video in the 90 days before March 2026 grew their revenue **50% faster** than those who hadn’t.

An in-person show can be filmed almost anywhere. ### What video podcast equipment do you need?

Start with your phone camera or computer’s built-in webcam. When you’re ready to spend money, prioritize a microphone: many people will only hear the episode in a podcast app, so sound quality matters more than a better camera.

- **Camera:** A phone camera or built-in webcam is enough. Consider an external webcam if the built-in camera looks grainy.
- **Light:** Face a window. In the evening, place a lamp behind the camera, pointing toward you.
- **Microphone:** Wired earbuds with a microphone work to start. A USB microphone costs about **$100–$300**; a clip-on microphone costs about **$60–$280** and keeps the microphone out of the picture.
- **Headphones:** Wear them with remote guests to prevent their voices from echoing into your microphone. Closed-back headphones cost about **$60–$200**.

See [podcast equipment for beginners](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/equipment) for a fuller list and price ranges.

### How to set up your video podcast recording space

A quiet room with a tidy background and light on your face is enough. Before recording:

- **Frame the shot:** Put the camera at eye level, about an arm’s length away. A stack of books under a laptop or phone works.
- **Keep your face near the center:** Substack makes portrait and landscape clips; portrait clips crop the sides of the frame.
- **Face the light:** Sit facing a window or lamp. A bright window behind you makes your face appear dark.
- **Choose your background:** A bookshelf, plant, or plain wall works. Remove anything you don’t want viewers to see.
- **Reduce noise and echo:** Turn off humming fans and appliances. Soft furniture, rugs, and curtains absorb echo.
- **Check your connection:** Use a stable internet connection for remote guests or livestreaming.

For room setup and sound testing, see [how to record a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/recording).

### How to record a video podcast

The **Substack Recording Studio** is free and built into Substack. It supports solo recording or up to **two guests**, adding your logo, and screen sharing. It works on the web and in the Substack app for iPhone and Android.

#### How to record in the Substack Recording Studio

1. Sign in on the web and select **Create → Recording studio**.
2. Allow access to your microphone and camera when prompted.
3. Invite guests using their Substack handles. A recording can have **three people total: you and two guests**. Guests can join from a computer or the Substack app.
4. To add a logo, select **Brand and effects**, turn on **Logo**, and choose top left, top right, or bottom left.
5. Select **Start recording**. Use **Share screen** to show slides, charts, or websites. Screen sharing works best in Google Chrome.
6. Select **End**. Substack creates a draft post containing the video and emails you when it is ready.

In the **Invite guests** panel, search by name or Substack handle. Guests receive invitations as a pop-up, push notification, or email.

Substack records each person in high resolution on their own computer or phone, then uploads the file when the session ends. The page says this prevents lag and dropped frames in the recording. In the draft, select **Switch to HD** to publish the high-resolution version.

Examples include Tara Palmeri adding her Red Letter logo to [an episode with congressional reporter Juliegrace Brufke](https://www.tarapalmeri.com/p/inside-the-gop-retreat-war-gas-prices), and Catherine Price customizing thumbnail text for [her conversation with author Dan Coyle](https://catherineprice.substack.com/p/learning-how-to-flourish-with-dan).

#### How to record a live video podcast

To record in front of an audience, select **Create → Live** on the web, or **+ → Live** in the Substack app.

- Up to **three people** can stream together, joining from computers or the Substack app.
- Choose whether everyone, all subscribers, or paid subscribers only can watch.
- After the stream, Substack saves the recording as a draft post that you can publish as an episode.
- To stream to YouTube simultaneously, turn on **Multicast to YouTube** before going live. Multicast works **from a computer, for livestreams open to everyone**.

### Edit and publish your episode

Every recording becomes a video post that can be published as a podcast episode. As an example, Rachel Braun used only Substack tools to record, publish, and clip [a Braun & Brains conversation with Express Checkout’s Nate Rosen](https://braunandbrains.substack.com/p/the-state-of-snacks-with-express).

Before publishing, check these video-editor settings:

- **Podcast audio:** Turn on **Add audio to podcast RSS feed**. People on Substack can watch the video, while listeners on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other podcast apps hear the episode. To use a higher-quality audio file, select the three dots, then **Replace**.
- **Transcript:** Every video post with audio receives an automatic transcript. Edit it or upload your own **.txt, .srt, or .vtt** file.
- **Thumbnail:** Upload an image or choose a still from the video.
- **Clips:** Select the scissors icon to see automatically generated clips, or make your own clip of up to **five minutes**.
- **Free preview:** For a paid episode, choose the portion everyone can watch. The same preview applies to audio in podcast apps. See [how to start a paid podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/paid-podcast).

If you recorded elsewhere, edit the file first, then select **Create → Video → Select file**. For fastest processing, Substack recommends **1080p or 1440p video**, **H.264 video and AAC audio**, and files up to **20 GB**. See [how to edit a podcast](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/editing) for cutting mistakes and long pauses.

Substack hosts video and audio episodes for free, with **no hosting fees and no platform fees**.

### Share your video podcast on YouTube, Spotify, and social media

Publishing once on Substack delivers an episode to subscribers by email and in the Substack app. Other distribution options include:

- **YouTube:** Connect your account under **Connected accounts** in publication settings. Video posts upload to YouTube when published and are **private by default**; you can choose unlisted or public. You can also select automatic clips to post as YouTube Shorts.
- **Spotify:** The audio goes to Spotify automatically when you publish a video episode. To show the video there too, upload it to the episode in your **Spotify for Creators** dashboard. See [how to get your podcast on Spotify](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/spotify).
- **Apple Podcasts and other podcast apps:** Listeners receive the audio through your podcast’s RSS feed. See [how to get your podcast on Apple Podcasts](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/apple-podcasts) and [what a podcast RSS feed is](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/rss-feed).
- **Social media:** Share clips as Substack Notes and to Instagram Stories and Reels from the Substack app. You can also upload clips to LinkedIn or download them as MP4 files. See [how to grow a podcast audience](https://substack.com/how-to-start-a-podcast/grow-audience).

For monetization, episodes and livestreams can be restricted to paid subscribers. Creators keep **90% of earnings, minus credit card fees**. Substack is also adding [podcast sponsorships](https://on.substack.com/p/introducing-podcast-sponsorships). **Dynamic sponsorships are in early access** and allow campaigns with your own sponsors and ad updates across the back catalog without re-editing episodes. ### Frequently asked questions

#### Do I need a camera to start a video podcast?

You do not need a separate camera: your phone camera or computer’s built-in webcam is enough. Put it at eye level and face a window or lamp. A clip-on microphone, about **$60–$280**, is a useful first upgrade because it stays out of the shot.

#### Can I record a video podcast for free?

Yes. The Substack Recording Studio is free and supports solo recording or up to two guests, a logo, and screen sharing. Substack also hosts and distributes episodes for free, with no hosting fees and no platform fees.

#### Should you start a video podcast or an audio podcast?

You can do both with one episode. Turn on **Add audio to podcast RSS feed** for a video post. People on Substack watch the video, while listeners on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other podcast apps hear the same episode.

#### How do I put my video podcast on YouTube?

Connect your YouTube account in your Substack publication’s settings. Substack uploads published video posts to your channel, and clips can also be posted as YouTube Shorts. **Verify your YouTube channel first to upload videos longer than 15 minutes.**
